questions.short_title: Salvage Convention - Article 13 Award Criteria, Duties and LOF 2000
questions.text_verbatim: A grounded ship has been re-floated and towed by a professional salvor to a place of safety. As per the Salvage Convention the salvor has a right to award. a) List the various criteria which are considered under Article 13 of the Convention for determining the amount of award (5) b) State the duties of the salvor and the shipowner/master as per this Convention (5) c) Assuming LOF-2000 was agreed between the parties, discuss when is the Convention applicable and when the LOF if any dispute arises. (6)

subparts.text: The criteria considered under Article 13 of the Convention in determining the amount of award.
The duties of the salvor and of the shipowner and master under the Convention.
Assuming LOF 2000 was agreed between the parties, when the Convention applies and when the LOF applies if a dispute arises.

blocks.h: 1. The Convention, and what the stem's facts have established

blocks.p: The governing instrument is the International Convention on Salvage, 1989, adopted at London and in force since 1996. It replaced the Brussels Convention of 1910 and, unlike its predecessor, is concerned with the marine environment as well as with property.

The facts in the stem matter and should be used, not skipped. A professional salvor has refloated a grounded ship and towed her to a place of safety. A useful result has been achieved, and that is the precondition for any payment at all. The stem is therefore correct that a right to an award has accrued.

Keep two articles apart from the first line, because the whole of limb (a) depends on it. Article 12 creates the entitlement - no useful result, no payment. Article 13 fixes the amount. A candidate who describes 'no cure, no pay' as an Article 13 principle has merged the two and will struggle to answer the rest cleanly. (The stem says award; the Convention says reward. They are the same thing and no mark turns on the word.)

Article 12 retains the old bargain intact: salvage operations which have had a useful result give a right to a reward, and operations which have had no useful result give no payment. No cure, no pay survives into the modern treaty.

Article 13 then says how the reward is fixed, and it opens with its own purpose: the reward shall be fixed with a view to encouraging salvage operations. That purpose is worth one sentence in the answer, because it explains why the list contains things - promptness, readiness, equipment kept available - that have nothing to do with how hard this particular job was. The treaty is paying for a standing capability, not only for a service.
Taking them in the Convention's own order:

ul: the salved value of the vessel and other property;
the skill and efforts of the salvors in preventing or minimising damage to the environment;
the measure of success obtained by the salvor;
the nature and degree of the danger;
the skill and efforts of the salvors in salving the vessel, other property and life;
the time used and the expenses and losses incurred by the salvors;
the risk of liability and other risks run by the salvors or their equipment;
the promptness of the services rendered;
the availability and use of vessels or other equipment intended for salvage operations;
the state of readiness and efficiency of the salvor's equipment and the value thereof.

blocks.p: Note where the environmental criterion sits - second, immediately after salved value. Under the 1910 Convention a salvor who prevented a spill but saved nothing earned nothing. Putting environmental effort near the top of the list is the 1989 Convention's answer to that, and it is the single most examinable feature of Article 13.

blocks.h: 4. How the criteria are applied, and what can reduce the award

ul: They are not listed in order of importance. The Convention says so expressly. A tribunal weighs all of them together; it does not work down a ranked list.

The reward may not exceed the salved value of the vessel and other property. This is the cap, and it is the reason a salvor of a low-value ship may recover far less than the operation cost him - which is the gap Article 14 special compensation was written to fill. Article 14 is not asked here and is not developed.

Payment is apportioned. The reward is paid by all the vessel and property interests in proportion to their respective salved values - so ship and cargo each contribute according to what each got back.

Article 18 - the salvor may be deprived of the whole or part of the payment where the salvage was made necessary or more difficult by his own fault or neglect, or where he has been guilty of fraud or other dishonest conduct.
Article 19 - services rendered notwithstanding the express and reasonable prohibition of the owner or master give rise to no payment.

blocks.p: These are set out in Article 8. The salvor owes a duty to the owner of the vessel and of the property in danger:

ul: to carry out the salvage operations with due care;
in performing that duty, to exercise due care to prevent or minimise damage to the environment;
whenever circumstances reasonably require, to seek assistance from other salvors;

to accept the intervention of other salvors when reasonably requested to do so by the owner or master of the vessel - though the amount of his own reward is not prejudiced should that request prove to have been unreasonable.

blocks.p: The last two exist because a salvor's commercial interest is to keep the job to himself, and the Convention will not let that interest run against the safety of the casualty.

blocks.h: 6. The duties of the shipowner and master, and why they are mutual

blocks.p: Article 8 imposes duties on the other side too, and this is the half candidates omit. The owner and master of the vessel owe the salvor:

ul: a duty to co-operate fully with him during the course of the salvage operations;
in doing so, a duty to exercise due care to prevent or minimise damage to the environment;
a duty to accept redelivery when the vessel or other property has been brought to a place of safety and redelivery is reasonably requested by the salvor.

blocks.p: The third of those is live on these facts. The stem has the ship towed to a place of safety, so the owner cannot leave her on the salvor's hands; once redelivery is reasonably requested he must take her back, and the salvage service ends there.

Two further points complete the limb. Article 6 gives the master authority to conclude a salvage contract on behalf of the owner of the vessel, and the master or owner authority to conclude one on behalf of the property on board - which is what makes a form signed at the height of a casualty binding on cargo interests who were never consulted. And the environmental duty is imposed on both sides in identical terms. That symmetry is the Convention's innovation, and saying so is what turns a list into an answer.

blocks.h: (c) LOF 2000, the Convention, and which governs
7. What LOF 2000 is, and what it is not

blocks.p: Lloyd's Open Form is a standard-form salvage contract. It is not an instrument, not a convention and not law. Getting that first sentence right is most of this limb.

ul: It is open in the sense that matters here: the remuneration is deliberately left unfixed at the moment of agreement. Nobody prices the job in the middle of a casualty.
It is written on the no cure, no pay basis, the same principle Article 12 states.
It is short and signed in minutes, commonly by the master under his Article 6 authority, so that work begins at once instead of after a negotiation.
It carries its own machinery - arbitration, security and appeal - and it may be supplemented by the SCOPIC clause, which is likewise a commercial contract and not part of the Convention.

blocks.h: 8. When the Convention applies, and when the LOF applies

blocks.p: The Convention applies by default. Where a Contracting State has given it force in its own law - India has, through the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 - its rules govern any salvage operation, whether or not a contract was made. It supplies the substantive law: the entitlement, the criteria, the duties, the cap and the apportionment.

But Article 6 makes the position more precise than 'the treaty always wins'. The Convention applies to any salvage operation save to the extent that a contract otherwise provides, expressly or by implication. So the parties may contract on their own terms - except that the Convention's protective provisions, in particular the duties in Article 8 and the environmental scheme, cannot be contracted out of.

The LOF applies where the parties agreed it, and on these facts they did. Within its scope it governs the relationship between them: it fixes the forum, the governing law, the provision of security, and the machinery by which the sum is determined. What it does not do is create the right to be paid. That comes from the Convention.

blocks.h: 9. How a dispute is actually resolved, and the relationship stated as a rule

blocks.p: If a dispute arises under an LOF, it does not go to the courts of the place where the ship went aground:

ul: it goes to arbitration in London under English law, under the form's own terms;
the salvor's claim is secured before the ship and cargo are released, so the owner cannot simply sail away from the argument;
the arbitrator fixes the amount by applying the Article 13 criteria - the same ten;
an appeal lies within the structure the form itself provides.

blocks.p: State the relationship as a rule and the limb is finished:

ul: the contract governs procedure and terms; the Convention governs substance;
where the contract is silent, the Convention fills the gap;
where the contract would defeat the Convention's protective provisions, the Convention prevails.

blocks.p: That is why the arrangement exists at all. A casualty needs a decision in minutes and a valuation that takes months. The form lets the work start; the Convention makes sure the sum is afterwards fixed on principled criteria. Between them they are the reason a professional salvor sails towards a ship that nobody has yet agreed to pay for.

The examiner has set three tasks and paid 5, 5 and 6. The six is on the LOF limb, which is the analytical one. That allocation should visibly change what you write: the ten criteria are worth half a mark each and deserve a tight list, while limb (c) deserves prose and a stated rule.

The opening separation of Article 12 (entitlement) from Article 13 (amount) costs one sentence and protects the whole answer. Ending limb (c) on a three-line rule rather than on a description is what distinguishes a pass from a good mark, because it answers the question the examiner actually asked - which one governs - instead of describing each in turn.

ul: Answering only the salvor's duties in limb (b). Half the marks are on the owner and master. The stem even signals it by naming them.
Treating LOF 2000 as an instrument. It is a contract. A candidate who writes 'under LOF 2000 the salvor is entitled to...' as though it were law has missed the limb.
Ranking the Article 13 criteria. They are expressly not in order of importance.
Drifting into Article 14 special compensation. It is not asked. Mention the cap at salved value and move on.
Forgetting the cap and the apportionment. They are cheap marks in limb (a) and are routinely omitted.
Missing the redelivery duty, which is the one duty the stem's own facts trigger.
'Place of safety' is not 'place of refuge'. The first is the Convention's trigger for redelivery; the second belongs to the IMO guidelines on places of refuge and to a different question entirely.
'The salvor has a right to award' is the paper's own wording, missing an article. It is not a hint that anything unusual is being asked.
The stem supplies LOF 2000 as a fact. Do not comment on whether a later edition of the form was in use - it is not asked, and it is not verifiable from the paper.
SCOPIC is a trap door. Name it in one line as a contractual supplement. A paragraph on it is a paragraph not spent on limb (c).
Indian law. India gave the Convention effect through the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. Say that; do not invent a section number.
What happens if the salvor saves nothing but prevents a major spill? (The Article 13 cap bites; Article 14 special compensation is the answer, and SCOPIC is the commercial fix.)
Who actually pays the award, and in what shares?
Can the master bind the cargo owner to an LOF he has never seen? (Article 6.)
Why arbitration in London and not the courts of the casualty's own country?
What is the difference between salvage and towage? (Danger, and voluntariness.)
Can a salvor be deprived of his reward? (Articles 18 and 19.)

blocks.p: Three questions, three blocks: how much, who must do what, which one governs.

For the ten criteria, run down the sentence VALUE - ENVIRONMENT - SUCCESS - DANGER - SKILL - TIME - RISK - PROMPTNESS - AVAILABILITY - READINESS. The first two are the ones to get right: salved value because it is also the cap, and environment because its position near the top of the list is the whole point of the 1989 Convention.
For limb (c), one line: the form routes the argument, the treaty decides it.

blocks.p: The Salvage Convention 1989 is not held by the True Source corpus. The corpus's liability-and-compensation family covers HNS, Nairobi, LLMC and the CLC/FUND/Bunkers group, and does not extend to Salvage. Every article identity and effect above is therefore authoritative secondary, carried through two MIW answers whose printed stems and content were read in full this session. No article is quoted, and no sub-paragraph below article level is asserted. The Article 13 criteria are given in the Convention's own order and count; the wording is paraphrase.

The contractual layer is deliberately under-specified. LOF and SCOPIC have each been revised more than once. LOF 2000 is named only because the stem supplies it, no other edition is named, no clause number is cited, and nothing is asserted about which form was in general commercial use in July 2023.

The Indian statutory link is stated at the level of identity only. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is not held by the corpus - the corpus holds the 2025 Act, which is future by roughly 32 months at this sitting - so no section number is given for the provision that gives the Convention effect.

questions.recurrence_adjudication: Adjudicated by reading both printed stems in full. 490 of 505 characters are identical; the divergence is confined to the three printed mark figures and to four words of limb c). This is a genuine recurrence of one examiner question across thirteen months, not two questions on one topic. It is recorded as NEAR rather than EXACT because a redistributed mark allocation is a real difference to a candidate writing against the clock, and MIW does not classify a marks change as cosmetic.

blocks.p: A ship goes aground. Nobody yet knows what the job will cost, how long it will take, or whether it will work at all - and the one thing that cannot be done is spend a fortnight negotiating a price while the ship sits on the ground. So the law and the market solved the problem from two ends at once, and this question is about how the two halves fit together.

The legal half starts from a simple bargain: rescue property at sea and you are paid; fail and you are not. That is old law and it survived into the modern treaty untouched. What the treaty added was a way of fixing how much - not a tariff, but a list of things a tribunal weighs up, so that a hard job in bad weather on a valuable ship is paid better than an easy tow. It also added something genuinely new: because the old bargain paid only for saved property, a salvor had no reason to care about oil going over the side, so the treaty made looking after the environment a duty on the salvor and on the shipowner, and made it one of the things the payment is measured against.

The commercial half is a one-page form the master can sign in minutes without agreeing any figure at all. That is its whole point. Work starts immediately and the money is argued about afterwards, in front of an arbitrator in London, using the treaty's own list of considerations.

So the rule to hold onto is this: the form decides where and how the argument happens; the treaty decides what the answer is measured against. The form does not create the right to be paid, and it cannot sign away the protections the treaty puts there deliberately. The third limb of this question is asking exactly that - which of the two governs, and when.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three separate legal tasks joined by one set of facts. LIMB a) is pure recall of a list and is marked as recall - five marks for ten criteria. LIMB b) is a two-sided duties question and the mark is lost by answering only the salvor's side. LIMB c) is the only analytical limb, is the best paid at six, and asks a relationship question: which of a treaty and a contract governs, and when. The stem's facts - grounded, refloated, towed to a place of safety by a professional salvor - are not decoration: they establish a useful result, which is the precondition for any award at all, and they trigger the owner's duty to accept redelivery.

decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate knows Article 13 is about QUANTUM and Article 12 about ENTITLEMENT, and does not merge them. That the ten criteria are given as a list, not as an essay. That the duties are recognised as MUTUAL - the Convention's innovation - rather than as obligations on the salvor alone. That LOF 2000 is identified as a CONTRACT and not as an instrument. That the candidate can state the relationship as a rule rather than describing each in turn and leaving them unconnected.

It is NOT the same as the 'place of refuge' concept in the IMO guidelines on places of refuge, and the answer does not conflate them. 'Award' and 'reward' are used interchangeably by the stem and by the Convention respectively; the answer notes this once and then follows the Convention.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Nine numbered sections under three limb headings. Limb (a) - the scheme, then the ten criteria as a single ordered list, then how they are applied. steps.title: The Convention, and what the stem's facts have established
points: International Convention on Salvage, 1989 - in force 1996, replacing the Brussels Convention of 1910
Grounded, refloated, towed to a place of safety by a professional salvor: a USEFUL RESULT has been achieved
Article 12 gives the entitlement; Article 13 fixes the amount. Do not merge them

steps.title: The scheme Article 13 sits inside
points: Article 12 - no payment without a useful result. NO CURE NO PAY is retained by the modern treaty
Article 13 - the reward is fixed with a view to ENCOURAGING SALVAGE OPERATIONS
The stem calls it an award; the Convention calls it a reward. Same thing

steps.title: The ten Article 13 criteria
points: Salved value; skill and efforts in preventing or minimising damage to the environment; measure of success
Nature and degree of the danger; skill and efforts in salving the vessel, other property and life; time used, expenses and losses incurred
Risk of liability and other risks run; promptness of the services; availability and use of vessels or other equipment; state of readiness, efficiency and value of the salvor's equipment

steps.title: How the criteria are applied, and what can reduce the award
points: They are NOT ranked in order of importance - all are taken together
The reward may not exceed the salved value of the vessel and other property; ship and cargo pay in PROPORTION to their salved values
Article 18 - the salvor's misconduct, fault or neglect may deprive him of all or part; Article 19 - services against express and reasonable prohibition are not payable

steps.title: The salvor's duties
points: Carry out the salvage operations with DUE CARE
In performing that duty, exercise due care to PREVENT OR MINIMISE DAMAGE TO THE ENVIRONMENT
Seek help from other salvors when circumstances reasonably require, and accept their intervention when reasonably requested by the owner or master

steps.title: The duties of the shipowner and master, and why they are mutual
points: Co-operate fully with the salvor, and in doing so exercise due care to prevent or minimise damage to the environment
ACCEPT REDELIVERY when the vessel has been brought to a place of safety and redelivery is reasonably requested - the duty the stem's facts trigger
Article 6 - the master may conclude a salvage contract on behalf of the owner of the vessel. The environmental duty binds BOTH sides, which is the Convention's innovation

steps.title: What LOF 2000 is, and what it is not
points: Lloyd's Open Form - a standard-form salvage CONTRACT, not an instrument and not law
No cure no pay; the remuneration is deliberately LEFT OPEN at the time of signature
Signed in minutes, often by the master under his Article 6 authority, so that work can begin at once

steps.title: When the Convention applies, and when the LOF applies
points: The Convention governs by default wherever a Contracting State has given it force, and supplies the substantive law
Article 6 - the Convention applies to any salvage operation SAVE AS OTHERWISE PROVIDED in a contract; but its protective provisions cannot be contracted out of
The LOF governs where the parties agreed it: it fixes forum, governing law, security and the machinery for fixing the sum

steps.title: How a dispute is actually resolved, and the relationship stated as a rule
points: Under the LOF: arbitration in London under English law, not litigation where the casualty happened; security given before the property is released; appeal within the form's own structure
The arbitrator fixes the amount by applying the ARTICLE 13 CRITERIA - so the form routes the dispute and the Convention decides it

THE RULE: the contract governs procedure and terms; the Convention governs substance. Where the contract is silent the Convention fills the gap; where the contract would defeat the Convention's protective provisions, the Convention prevails

questions.memory_cue: Three questions, three answers: HOW MUCH (2-4), WHO MUST DO WHAT (5-6), WHICH ONE GOVERNS (7-9). For the ten criteria use VALUE - ENVIRONMENT - SUCCESS - DANGER - SKILL - TIME - RISK - PROMPTNESS - AVAILABILITY - READINESS, written out at step 3.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Salvage Convention 1989, in force 1996, replaced Brussels 1910, UNAMENDED. Article 12 = entitlement (useful result; no cure no pay). Article 13 = amount. TEN CRITERIA, expressly NOT ranked: salved value; skill and efforts in preventing or minimising environmental damage; measure of success; nature and degree of danger; skill and efforts in salving vessel, property and life; time used, expenses and losses; risk of liability and other risks; promptness; availability and use of vessels and equipment; state of readiness, efficiency and value of equipment. CAPPED at salved value; paid by ship and cargo in PROPORTION to salved values. Article 18 misconduct reduces or extinguishes; Article 19 services against express and reasonable prohibition earn nothing. ARTICLE 8 DUTIES, BOTH SIDES - salvor: due care, prevent or minimise environmental damage, seek other salvors when reasonably required, accept their intervention when reasonably requested; owner and master: co-operate fully, due care for the environment, ACCEPT REDELIVERY at a place of safety. Article 6: master may bind the owner. LOF 2000 is a CONTRACT - no cure no pay, sum left open, arbitration in London under English law, security before release. THE RULE: contract governs procedure and terms, Convention governs substance; silence is filled by the Convention; the Convention prevails over a term that would defeat its protective provisions.
critical_numbers: Ten criteria in Article 13
Convention adopted 1989, in force 1996
Reward capped at the salved value of vessel and other property
Marks on this sitting: 5 + 5 + 6, the six on the LOF limb
quick_revision.critical_regulation: International Convention on Salvage, 1989 - Articles 6, 8, 12, 13, 18 and 19. LOF 2000 is a commercial contract and not part of the Convention.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering limb (b) on the salvor alone. Article 8 imposes duties on the SHIPOWNER AND MASTER as well - co-operate fully, exercise due care for the environment, and accept redelivery once the ship is at a place of safety - and the stem's own facts trigger the redelivery duty. The second trap is calling LOF 2000 an instrument: it is a contract, and limb (c) is asking precisely how a contract and a treaty relate.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Article 12 and Article 13 of the Salvage Convention - what does each do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 12 creates the ENTITLEMENT: salvage operations with a useful result give a right to a reward, and operations with no useful result give no payment - no cure, no pay. Article 13 fixes the AMOUNT, by reference to ten criteria and with a view to encouraging salvage operations. Merging the two is the commonest framing error on this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the ten Article 13 criteria in the Convention's order.
retrieval_cards.answer: Salved value; skill and efforts in preventing or minimising damage to the environment; measure of success; nature and degree of the danger; skill and efforts in salving vessel, other property and life; time used and expenses and losses incurred; risk of liability and other risks run; promptness; availability and use of vessels or other equipment; state of readiness, efficiency and value of the salvor's equipment.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are the Article 13 criteria applied in order of importance, and is there any ceiling on the reward?
retrieval_cards.answer: They are expressly NOT in order of importance - all are taken together. The reward may not exceed the salved value of the vessel and other property, and it is paid by the vessel and property interests in proportion to their respective salved values.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Article 8 - what does the SHIPOWNER OR MASTER owe the salvor?
retrieval_cards.answer: To co-operate fully with him during the salvage operations; in doing so to exercise due care to prevent or minimise damage to the environment; and to accept redelivery when the vessel or property has been brought to a place of safety and redelivery is reasonably requested. The environmental duty binds both sides in identical terms - the Convention's innovation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is LOF 2000, and what is it not?
retrieval_cards.answer: Lloyd's Open Form - a standard-form salvage CONTRACT on a no cure, no pay basis, in which the remuneration is deliberately left open at signature. It is not an instrument and not law. It is signed in minutes, often by the master under his Article 6 authority, and it carries arbitration in London under English law, provision of security, and an appeal structure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When a dispute arises under an LOF, which governs - the form or the Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: Both, in different registers. The contract governs procedure and terms - forum, governing law, security, machinery. The Convention governs substance: the arbitrator fixes the sum by applying the Article 13 criteria. Where the contract is silent the Convention fills the gap, and where a term would defeat the Convention's protective provisions the Convention prevails.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What can reduce or extinguish a salvor's payment?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 18 - the salvage was made necessary or more difficult by the salvor's own fault or neglect, or he has been guilty of fraud or other dishonest conduct. Article 19 - services rendered notwithstanding the express and reasonable prohibition of the owner or master give rise to no payment at all.

blocks.h: 1. What this inspection is, and the authority for it

blocks.p: It is worth one sentence to say what kind of exercise this is, because everything after it follows. This is a familiarisation and takeover inspection, made under the Company's safety management system. It is not a statutory survey, it is not a class survey and it is not an ISM audit. Its purpose is that the incoming Chief Engineer knows the true condition of the plant before he becomes answerable for it.

The authority is the ISM Code, which requires the Company to establish procedures to ensure that personnel new to a ship are given proper familiarisation with their duties before the ship sails, and which makes the Company responsible for ensuring the ship is manned by people who are properly qualified and familiarised. STCW reinforces it with a separate on-board familiarisation requirement. The takeover itself is a documented SMS procedure and ends in a signed handover.

One idea governs the whole inspection. The certificates already assert that the equipment exists and was working when the surveyor saw it. The Chief Engineer is looking for something different: has it been operated recently, by someone on board, and is there a record of it? Existence is on the Record of Equipment. Condition is in the logs, and in the machine.

Before going below, take ten minutes with the paperwork: the Passenger Ship Safety Certificate and its Record of Equipment, the class status with any conditions of class or memoranda, the last port State control report, the standing defects list, and the outstanding items from the last survey. That tells you where to look hard.

blocks.h: 2. Ship stability - the documents, the instrument and the lightship

blocks.p: On a passenger ship the stability case is not only about how she is loaded today; it is the foundation of the damage case in the next section. Inspect in this order:
The approved documents.

ul: The Stability Information Booklet, approved by the Administration, in a language the officers understand - containing the intact and damage stability particulars, the approved loading conditions, the limiting KG or GM curve and the tank capacities and free-surface data.
The damage control information derived from the same calculations, which is what the next limb depends on.
The subdivision load lines and the certificate that assigns them - a passenger ship carries more than one, and the officer of the watch must know which applies.

blocks.p: The instrument. Verify that the approved loading and stability instrument is the one named in the approval document, that it is functioning, and that the approved test conditions have been run at the required intervals with the results recorded and within tolerance. Check that the crew can operate it, and that there is a documented alternative means of demonstrating compliance if it fails.

The standard she is held to. A passenger ship is subject to the probabilistic damage stability regime of SOLAS chapter II-1, not to a two-compartment rule of thumb, and to the intact criteria of the Intact Stability Code - which for passenger ships include the specific passenger-crowding and turning heeling criteria. Establish which regime her keel date puts her under; an older ship may be on the earlier deterministic standard and her booklet will say so.

The lightship. This is the passenger-ship point most often missed. The ship's whole stability case rests on her lightweight and centre of gravity, and accumulated modification changes both. A passenger ship must have a lightweight survey at periodical intervals not exceeding five years to check for deviation from the approved lightship data. Sight the date of the last one, the deviation recorded, and whether a re-inclining was required. Then check that recent modifications - a refit, new accommodation, added equipment - have been entered in the weight-change record.

Finally, look at the tanks: sounding and gauging arrangements accurate and calibrated, remote gauges cross-checked against manual soundings, and slack tanks minimised in the ballast plan, because free surface is the cheapest way to lose the margin the booklet assumes.

blocks.h: 3. Damage control - plans, watertight boundaries and the means to use them

blocks.p: Damage control on a passenger ship is the practical half of the stability case: the ship is designed to survive flooding, but only if the boundaries are actually intact and the crew can act.
The plans and the booklet.

ul: Damage control plans permanently exhibited for the guidance of the officer in charge, showing the watertight compartments, their openings and the means of closing them, and the arrangements for correcting list from flooding.
A damage control booklet available to the officers, in the ship's working language.
A duplicate set held ashore with the Company - verify it exists and is current, because it is what the emergency response service will work from.
The muster list and emergency organisation naming who does what, and the damage control training manual.

blocks.p: The watertight boundaries themselves. This is where an inspection earns its keep, because a plan is worth nothing if a door is chocked open:

ul: Power-operated watertight sliding doors - test local operation both sides, remote closing from the bridge, and the audible and visual alarm that sounds before and during closure. Check the closing time and the hand-gear.
The indicator panel on the bridge showing every door open or closed, and every shell, bow, stern and side door - and confirm the indication is real rather than a lamp that has been jumpered.

The sea-going regime. Watertight doors are to be kept closed at sea; establish the ship's standing orders on the few that may be opened, the permission required, and the log entry that records it. Verify the record of the periodical operation and inspection of watertight doors.
Shell doors, bow and stern doors and their securing arrangements, with indicators and where fitted the leakage detection and surveillance - the direct legacy of the ro-ro passenger ship losses.
Cross-flooding arrangements - the valves, their accessibility, their marking, and the written instructions for their use, including the time to equalise.

blocks.p: The means to pump and to know. Inspect the bilge pumping and drainage system - pump capacities, the emergency bilge suction in the machinery space, non-return and isolating valves, strainers and level alarms - and confirm the onboard stability computer with a damage-stability capability, or the shore-based damage-stability support service, is available, current and has been tested. That facility is a passenger-ship requirement and is the tool that turns a flooding casualty into a calculable one.
Finally, ask when the ship last held a damage control drill, and read the record rather than the answer.

blocks.h: 4. Firefighting - containment first, then the systems that fight it

blocks.p: Take structural containment before appliances. On a passenger ship the design intent is that a fire is confined to the space and the zone in which it starts; a candidate who begins with extinguishers has answered a cargo-ship question.
Containment.

ul: Main vertical zones and the A-class boundaries that form them - inspect for penetrations made during refit and never made good, which is the commonest real defect on any ship.
Fire doors - self-closing, held on releases that drop them on the fire alarm, tested from the control station and locally; no wedges, no hooks.
Dampers and ventilation closures, remote stops for ventilation fans, and the closing arrangements for skylights and openings to machinery spaces.

Means of escape from every space, in particular the second means from the machinery spaces; escape routes clear, marked, and fitted with low-location lighting; emergency escape breathing devices at their marked stations.
Fire control plans permanently exhibited, with the duplicate set in a prominently marked weathertight enclosure outside the deckhouse for the shore fire service.

blocks.p: Detection and fixed systems.

ul: Fixed fire detection and alarm throughout accommodation, service and control spaces, and the automatic sprinkler system required in those spaces on ships carrying more than 36 passengers - check the pressure tank, the pump auto-start on pressure drop, the section valves and the last section test.

The fixed fire-extinguishing system for the machinery spaces - identify the type installed and inspect its release station, the alarm that sounds before release, the ventilation and quick-closing valve interlocks, the bottle weighing or level check dates and the last servicing certificate.

Remote stops - fuel pumps, purifiers, ventilation fans - and the quick-closing valves on fuel and lubricating oil tanks, operated from their remote station and reset, which is the test most often skipped.
Fire pumps, their number and capacity, the emergency fire pump with its independent power and its isolating valve, hydrants, hoses and nozzles, and the international shore connection.

Firefighter's outfits and breathing apparatus - a passenger ship carries additional sets; check the counts against the Record of Equipment, the cylinder pressures, the recharging arrangement and the spare charges.

blocks.p: The safety centre. On a passenger ship the safety centre is the space from which the safety systems are controlled and monitored in an emergency. Go and sit in it. Verify that the indications work, that the controls operate, and that the officers can actually use them.

The paperwork that proves it. The maintenance and testing plan for the fire protection and fire-fighting systems, the servicing certificates for the fixed installations and the portable appliances, and the drill records - a passenger ship musters her crew weekly and musters embarking passengers within a short fixed period of departure. Read the records, and check the last drill included the machinery space.

blocks.h: 5. Critical machinery - the list, the redundancy and the proof it has been run

blocks.p: Start from the definition, because the examiner is looking for it. The ISM Code requires the Company to identify equipment and technical systems the sudden operational failure of which may result in hazardous situations, to provide specific measures to promote their reliability, and to include testing at regular intervals of stand-by arrangements and equipment or systems not in continuous use. That last clause is the whole of limb (iv) in one line: the standby half of every pair is what fails, precisely because it is not running.

Step one - verify the list itself. Obtain the Company's critical equipment list for this ship and check that it is ship-specific rather than a fleet template, that it names systems and not just machines, and that each entry has a defined test interval and a record of the last test.
Step two - inspect the entries, working outward from the consequences of failure.

rows: Steering gear

Main and auxiliary units and their changeover; the emergency steering position and communications; the alarm set; the alternative power supply that comes on automatically within 45 seconds where the rudder stock requires it; the records of the tests before departure and of the emergency steering drills
Main propulsion and its controls
Bridge control and changeover to local and to emergency control, the safety and slowdown system and any standing overrides, the last full manoeuvring test
Electrical power
Generator capacity against the load with one set out; blackout recovery and the last blackout test; preferential trip settings; the main switchboard's condition
Emergency generator

Automatic start and connection within the required time, on-load test records, fuel supply independent and full, ready-use tank, starting arrangements, and the transitional source. Verify the endurance the ship is certificated for - a passenger ship's is materially longer than a cargo ship's
Fire and bilge pumps
Started and run from their remote stations, not merely turned over locally
Watertight door power and its standby
Tested with the ship's power, and on the emergency source
Boilers, air compressors, starting air
Safety valve settings and last lift dates, starting air receiver pressure and number of starts available, compressor auto-start
Fuel and lubricating oil
Purifiers, filters, the transfer system, quick-closing valves and the tank high-level alarms
Thrusters and stabilisers where fitted
Availability, and their effect on the manoeuvring the passenger trade actually requires

blocks.p: Step three - establish which regime the ship falls under. Passenger ships above a size threshold, constructed after a fixed date, are subject to safe return to port: after a casualty below a defined threshold the ship must be able to return to port under her own power with specified systems remaining operational, and above it must permit orderly evacuation. This changes what counts as critical. Establish from the ship's construction date and dimensions whether she is inside that regime, and if she is, obtain the documentation identifying the systems required to remain available and verify their segregation and redundancy.

Step four - the maintenance evidence. The planned maintenance system up to date with no large block of overdue jobs; the critical spares on board and matched to the actual machinery; the survey status with any conditions of class; and the standing defect list with each item owned by someone and dated.

blocks.h: 6. Recording the findings, and closing them out

ul: Record findings in the safety management system as non-conformities or observations, with dates and owners - not in a private notebook, which leaves the Company no obligation and the next Chief Engineer no history.

Sign the handover document with the outgoing Chief Engineer, formally accepting the defect list, the conditions of class, the outstanding port State control items and the bunker and spares inventories.
Agree a priority plan with the Master and report it to the Company, distinguishing what must be corrected before sailing from what can be planned.

Anything that affects the ship's seaworthiness or her certificates is raised before departure, in writing. On a passenger ship that judgement is made against the number of people on board, not against the commercial schedule.

blocks.p: Four heads are printed and the answer gives them four blocks in the printed order. That alone secures the structure marks. The framing section at the start and the close-out at the end are deliberately short - they are worth little individually, but without them the answer is a list of equipment rather than an account of an inspection, and the examiner has asked for an inspection.

Within each head the order is the same: documents, then physical checks, then the records and tests to be sighted. That repetition is what lets a candidate write four blocks quickly under time pressure without having to invent a shape for each one.

ul: Answering it as a cargo ship question. If nothing in the answer is specific to a passenger ship - no main vertical zones, no sprinklers, no lightweight survey interval, no safety centre, no safe return to port - the candidate has not answered this question.
Starting limb (iii) with extinguishers. Containment comes first on a passenger ship.
Producing a critical equipment list from memory instead of naming the ISM Code requirement that creates it. The definition is worth more than three extra items on the list.
Checking that equipment exists rather than that it has been operated. The Record of Equipment already establishes existence.
Omitting the lightweight survey in limb (i). It is the one stability item peculiar to passenger ships and it is regularly missed.
Writing an ISM audit. The question asks what you inspect, not how you verify the system.

Safe return to port applies by date and size, not to every passenger ship. A candidate who asserts it for any passenger ship has over-claimed. State the thresholds and say the Chief Engineer establishes which side his ship falls.
The sprinkler requirement is tied to the number of passengers carried, and the threshold is more than 36. Do not state it as universal.

Damage stability for passenger ships is probabilistic under the current regime, but an older ship may be certificated on the earlier deterministic standard. The booklet settles it, not the candidate's assumption.
'Critical machinery' is an ISM concept, not a SOLAS term. Say so.
Watertight doors are to be kept closed at sea. Describing a regime in which they are normally open, with the bridge closing them in an emergency, is the wrong way round.
The duplicate fire control plan lives outside the deckhouse, in a marked weathertight enclosure, for the shore fire brigade - not on the bridge.
You find a watertight door wedged open on passage. What do you do, and what do you write?
The emergency generator starts but will not take load. Is the ship seaworthy?
How would you satisfy yourself that the loading instrument is giving correct answers?
Why does a passenger ship need a lightweight survey when a cargo ship does not?
What is the difference between the safety centre and the engine control room?
Your predecessor has left twenty-two open defects. How do you take over?
Which of the fixed fire systems on board would you test first, and why not the others?

blocks.p: Work outward from the water, and the four heads fall into order on their own:

ul: Does she float upright now? - stability: booklet, instrument, lightship.
Does she float upright after a hole? - damage control: plans, doors, cross-flooding, pumping.
Does a fire stay where it started? - firefighting: zones and boundaries first, then systems.
Will the machinery cause the emergency? - critical equipment: the list, the redundancy, the test record.

blocks.p: Then one sentence to open (what this inspection is) and one to close (write it down and hand it over).

rows: ISM Code

The authority for the inspection: familiarisation of new personnel before sailing; and the critical-equipment requirement that governs limb (iv), including testing of standby arrangements not in continuous use
STCW
The separate on-board familiarisation obligation
SOLAS chapter II-1

Subdivision and damage stability; stability information; the loading instrument; the lightweight survey; watertight integrity and watertight doors; damage control plans and booklet; bilge pumping; the onboard stability computer or shore-based damage-stability support
SOLAS II-1/29

Steering gear - main and auxiliary, the alternative power supply automatic within 45 seconds where the rudder stock requires it, and the testing regime. Read against primary text and recorded unamended
SOLAS II-1/42
Emergency source of electrical power, its capacity and duration, heel and trim conditions, and periodic testing. Read against primary text and recorded unamended
SOLAS chapter II-2

FSS Code
The construction and performance standards for the systems inspected under limb (iii)
SOLAS chapter III
Musters, drills and their records, and the LSA on board
Intact Stability Code
The intact criteria, including the passenger-crowding and turning criteria

blocks.p: The corpus holds a LATER edition of SOLAS than this sitting requires. The True Source corpus at 319524c holds the Consolidated Edition 2024, incorporating amendments in effect on 1 July 2024 - twelve months after this paper. That is the standing register inversion of the 2023 batch. It has been handled by relying on the held text only where the provision is recorded as unamended between the two dates, which is the case for II-1/29 and II-1/42. Those two carry primary support; everything else here is authoritative secondary.

No regulation is quoted and no paragraph number below regulation level is asserted, except where the corpus's own verification record establishes it. Two figures are given with that support: the 45-second automatic changeover for the steering gear alternative power supply, and the rudder-stock threshold that triggers it.

Thresholds stated as thresholds, not applied. The sprinkler requirement (more than 36 passengers), the safe-return-to-port regime (a construction date and a size or zone threshold) and the probabilistic damage stability regime (a construction date) are all conditional. The answer states the condition and directs the Chief Engineer to establish which side his ship falls, because the question supplies no ship particulars and any assumption would be invented.

The emergency power endurance figure is given as a comparison and not as a number. A passenger ship's required duration is materially longer than a cargo ship's; the exact figure is on the ship's own certificate and is not asserted here from a later edition.

questions.subpart_marks_note: The question prints a single total of (16) and no limb marks; the four heads (i) to (iv) are printed inline within the stem rather than as separately marked limbs. Limb marks are recorded as null rather than inferred as 4+4+4+4. The answer nonetheless plans four roughly equal blocks, because four named heads under one equal-marks total is the only reading the rubric supports.
questions.recurrence_adjudication: No recurrence anywhere in the 315-question set. The host annotation shows four sittings between 2010 and 2012, so this is a question the examiner has returned to over more than a decade, but MIW holds none of those papers and therefore holds no donor. Recorded as FRESH on a searched nil.

blocks.p: You have just walked up the gangway of a ship you have never seen, and from the moment you sign on you are answerable for her machinery. The question is what you go and look at, and in what order. It is not an audit and it is not a survey - it is the work of finding out, quickly and systematically, whether the ship you have inherited is actually in the condition her certificates say she is.

Why a passenger ship changes the answer. On a cargo ship, if something fails badly you get the crew off. On a ship full of passengers you cannot; the standing assumption in her design is that she is her own best lifeboat, so she is built to take damage and stay upright, to contain a fire inside one part of herself, and to keep the things that matter working after a casualty. Every one of the four heads in the question is a piece of that same idea, which is why the examiner named those four and not others.

So read the four heads as one chain rather than four topics. Stability is whether she floats upright as loaded now, and it lives in paperwork and in a computer. Damage control is whether she still floats upright after a hole, and it lives in plans on bulkheads and in doors that must actually close. Firefighting is whether a fire stays where it started, and it lives in fixed installations, boundaries and escape routes. Critical machinery is the list of things whose sudden failure would create the emergency in the first place, and the proof that the standby half of each pair has recently been run.

The unifying idea worth carrying into the exam room: you are not looking for whether the equipment exists - the certificates already say it does. You are looking for whether it has been operated recently, by someone, and whether there is a record of it. That is the difference between a Chief Engineer's inspection and a tour of the ship.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A four-part procedural question with a role attached. The examiner wants a systematic, prioritised inspection - not a list of equipment. Two things distinguish a good answer: that the four heads are treated as PASSENGER-SHIP heads rather than generic ones, and that the inspection is expressed as verification of CONDITION AND RECORD rather than of existence. The words 'new Chief Engineer' and 'on joining' are the two load-bearing phrases: they set the authority for the inspection (familiarisation and takeover, not survey) and they set the time pressure.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 printed as a single total, with four named heads and no limb marks. Planned as four roughly equal blocks of about four marks each, preceded by a short section establishing what the inspection is and under what authority, and closed by a short section on recording and closing out findings. The opening and closing sections are deliberately brief - they frame the answer and they are not where the marks are.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate knows what is passenger-ship specific: probabilistic damage stability and the lightweight survey interval; the damage control plan and booklet and the watertight door regime; sprinklers, main vertical zones, low-location lighting and the safety centre; and the safe-return-to-port regime with its date and size thresholds. That the ISM Code paragraph on critical equipment is named as the authority for limb (iv) rather than a list being produced from memory. That the answer distinguishes what the Chief Engineer verifies HIMSELF from what he verifies through records.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: The True Source corpus at 319524c holds SOLAS as the CONSOLIDATED EDITION 2024 - one edition LATER than this sitting - plus the ISM Code, LSA Code and FSS Code. Two provisions relied on here have been read against that primary text and recorded as UNAMENDED through 2026, which is what makes the later edition safe to use for a July 2023 sitting: II-1/29 (steering gear) and II-1/42 (emergency electrical power). Those two are P1. Everything else in this answer - the passenger-ship damage stability regime, the damage control plan requirement, the sprinkler and safety-centre requirements, the safe-return-to-port thresholds - is P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY, given by regulation identity and effect with NO TEXT QUOTED.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW - nothing in the four heads moved between July 2023 and the present. The passenger-ship damage stability regime has been probabilistic since 1 January 2020; safe return to port has applied since 1 July 2010; the safety centre requirement dates from the same set. The one edition hazard is the reverse of the usual: the corpus holds the SOLAS 2024 consolidated edition, which is FUTURE by twelve months at this sitting, so the answer cites the 2020 consolidated edition as the one in the ship's own bookcase in July 2023 and relies on the 2024 text only where the provision is recorded as unamended.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW - the question is SOLAS and ISM, both of which apply to an Indian-flag passenger ship on international voyages without modification. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is the enabling statute and is named once, by identity, with no section asserted. Domestic Indian passenger vessels on non-international voyages are outside the question and are not discussed.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: 'Critical machinery' has no SOLAS definition. The ISM Code speaks of equipment and technical systems the sudden operational failure of which may result in hazardous situations, and that is the definition used - stated as such rather than presented as a SOLAS term. 'Firefighting' in the stem covers both fire PROTECTION (boundaries, escapes) and fire FIGHTING (systems, appliances); the answer takes both, because a passenger-ship answer confined to extinguishers would miss the main vertical zone concept entirely. The safe-return-to-port regime applies by keel date and size, so the answer states the thresholds and says the Chief Engineer must first establish which side of them his ship falls, rather than assuming.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Six numbered sections: one framing the inspection and its authority, four on the named heads in the printed order, one on recording and close-out. Each of the four central sections opens with what the head is FOR on a passenger ship, then gives the documents, then the physical checks, then the records and tests to be sighted.

steps.title: What this inspection is, and the authority for it
points: A familiarisation and takeover inspection under the ISM Code, NOT a survey and NOT an audit
ISM Code - the Company must establish procedures for new personnel to become familiar with their duties before sailing
The governing question throughout: not does it exist, but has it been operated recently and is there a record

steps.title: Ship stability - the documents, the instrument and the lightship
points: Approved Stability Information Booklet and the approved loading and stability instrument, with its test conditions run
Passenger ships are subject to PROBABILISTIC damage stability; the intact criteria include the passenger-crowding and turning criteria
The LIGHTWEIGHT SURVEY interval for passenger ships - not exceeding five years - and the current deadweight and lightship data

steps.title: Damage control - plans, watertight boundaries and the means to use them
points: Damage control plans permanently exhibited and the damage control booklet available, in the working language, with a duplicate ashore
Watertight doors: indication on the bridge, local and central closing, the sea-going regime, and the closing test
Cross-flooding arrangements, bilge and drainage, shell and bow door indicators, and the onboard stability computer or shore-based damage-stability support

steps.title: Firefighting - containment first, then the systems that fight it
points: Structural containment: main vertical zones, A-class boundaries, fire doors and their release, means of escape and low-location lighting
Fixed systems and their release stations, ventilation and quick-closing valve shutdowns and remote stops; sprinkler and detection coverage; fire pumps including the emergency pump
The SAFETY CENTRE, the fire control plan and its shore-side duplicate, the maintenance and testing plan, and the servicing records

steps.title: Critical machinery - the list, the redundancy and the proof it has been run
points: The ISM Code critical-equipment requirement: identify systems whose sudden failure may create a hazard, and TEST at regular intervals what is not in continuous use
Verify the Company's ship-specific list, then the redundancy behind each entry - steering gear, emergency generator, blackout recovery, fire pumps, watertight door power
Establish whether the ship is subject to SAFE RETURN TO PORT, because that changes which systems must survive a casualty

steps.title: Recording the findings, and closing them out
points: Findings entered in the SMS as non-conformities or observations, not in a private notebook
Handover document signed with the outgoing Chief Engineer; defects list, conditions of class and outstanding PSC deficiencies formally accepted
Priority plan agreed with the Master and reported to the Company, with anything affecting seaworthiness raised before sailing

questions.memory_cue: Work outward from the water: FLOATS UPRIGHT NOW (2), FLOATS UPRIGHT AFTER DAMAGE (3), FIRE STAYS PUT (4), MACHINERY DOES NOT CAUSE THE EMERGENCY (5). Frame it at (1), write it down at (6).

quick_revision.recall_15s: A FAMILIARISATION AND TAKEOVER INSPECTION under the ISM Code - not a survey, not an audit. The governing test throughout: not does it exist, but HAS IT BEEN OPERATED RECENTLY AND IS THERE A RECORD. (i) STABILITY - approved Stability Information Booklet; approved loading and stability instrument with its test conditions run; probabilistic damage stability regime; Intact Stability Code criteria including passenger crowding and turning; LIGHTWEIGHT SURVEY at intervals not exceeding five years; subdivision load lines; tank gauging and free surface. (ii) DAMAGE CONTROL - damage control plans permanently exhibited, booklet in the working language, duplicate ashore; watertight doors tested locally, remotely and by hand, with bridge indication, alarms and the KEPT-CLOSED-AT-SEA regime; shell, bow and stern door indicators; cross-flooding valves and instructions; bilge pumping and emergency bilge suction; onboard stability computer with damage-stability capability or shore-based support; damage control drill record. (iii) FIREFIGHTING - CONTAINMENT FIRST: main vertical zones, A-class boundaries, penetrations made good, fire doors on releases, dampers and remote fan stops, means of escape with low-location lighting, EEBDs; THEN SYSTEMS: detection and alarm, sprinklers where more than 36 passengers are carried, the machinery-space fixed system with its release station and interlocks, remote stops and quick-closing valves, fire pumps and the emergency fire pump, international shore connection, firefighter's outfits; the SAFETY CENTRE; fire control plan with the duplicate OUTSIDE THE DECKHOUSE; maintenance and testing plan, servicing certificates and drill records. (iv) CRITICAL MACHINERY - the ISM Code requirement to identify systems whose SUDDEN OPERATIONAL FAILURE may create a hazard and to TEST STANDBY ARRANGEMENTS NOT IN CONTINUOUS USE; verify the ship-specific list; steering gear with its alternative power automatic within 45 seconds; blackout recovery; emergency generator on load; fire and bilge pumps from remote stations; watertight door power on the emergency source; establish whether SAFE RETURN TO PORT applies by construction date and size. CLOSE OUT: findings into the SMS, signed handover, priority plan to the Master and the Company.
keywords: fire control plan outside the deckhouse
critical_numbers: Lightweight survey for passenger ships at intervals not exceeding five years
Sprinkler requirement applies to ships carrying more than 36 passengers
Steering gear alternative power supply automatic within 45 seconds where the rudder stock requires it
A passenger ship's emergency power endurance is materially longer than a cargo ship's - read it off her certificate
Four printed heads under one printed total of 16
quick_revision.critical_regulation: ISM Code - familiarisation of new personnel before sailing, and the identification and periodic testing of critical equipment including standby arrangements not in continuous use. SOLAS chapters II-1, II-2 and III with the FSS Code supply the passenger-ship requirements inspected under each head.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering it as a cargo ship. The examiner named a PASSENGER ship and four heads that are all pieces of the same design idea - that she must survive her own casualty because the people cannot be taken off. An answer with no main vertical zones, no sprinkler threshold, no lightweight survey, no safety centre and no safe return to port has missed what the question is for. The second trap is checking that equipment EXISTS rather than that it has been OPERATED and recorded.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Under the ISM Code, what makes a piece of equipment 'critical', and what does the Code require be done about it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Equipment and technical systems the sudden operational failure of which may result in hazardous situations. The Company must identify them, provide specific measures to promote their reliability, and include in its procedures the testing at regular intervals of stand-by arrangements and of equipment or systems not in continuous use.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How often must a passenger ship have a lightweight survey, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: At periodical intervals not exceeding five years, to check for deviation from the approved lightship displacement and longitudinal centre of gravity. It matters because the entire intact and damage stability case is built on the lightship figures, and accumulated modification changes them without anyone recalculating.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What do you check on a power-operated watertight sliding door, and what is the sea-going regime?
retrieval_cards.answer: Local operation from both sides, remote closing from the bridge, hand-gear, closing time, and the audible and visual alarm before and during closure; then the bridge indicator panel showing the true position of every door. Watertight doors are to be kept CLOSED at sea; check the standing orders on the few that may be opened, the permission required, the log entry, and the record of periodical operation and inspection.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In what order do you inspect fire safety on a passenger ship, and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: Containment first, then systems. Main vertical zones and A-class boundaries (looking for refit penetrations never made good), fire doors on releases, dampers and remote fan stops, means of escape with low-location lighting. Only then detection, sprinklers, the machinery-space fixed system, remote stops and quick-closing valves, fire pumps and outfits. The design intent on a passenger ship is that fire is confined to the zone it starts in, so containment is the primary defence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does safe return to port apply to every passenger ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It applies by construction date and by size - passenger ships built on or after a fixed date and of a defined length, or having a defined number of main vertical zones. The Chief Engineer establishes from the ship's particulars which side of the threshold she falls, and if she is inside it obtains the documentation identifying which systems must remain operational after a casualty.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where must the fire control plans be, on a passenger ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: Permanently exhibited on board for the guidance of the officers; and a duplicate set in a prominently marked weathertight enclosure OUTSIDE the deckhouse, for the assistance of shore-side firefighting personnel.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between this inspection and an ISM internal audit?
retrieval_cards.answer: The audit tests whether the safety management SYSTEM is being followed and is effective. This inspection establishes the actual CONDITION of the plant so that the incoming Chief Engineer knows what he has become answerable for. It is carried out under an SMS familiarisation and handover procedure and ends in a signed handover, not in an audit report.
