blocks.h: 1. The legal frame - which instruments govern a collision claim

blocks.p: Three bodies of law meet in a collision claim and it is worth naming them before the limbs, because each limb draws on a different one.

ul: The Collision Convention of 1910 - the Brussels convention for the unification of certain rules of law with respect to collisions between vessels - is the source of the modern doctrine on apportionment and on presumptions. It is unamended, and it is the instrument all four limbs of this question are really about.
The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is the Indian statute through which those rules have effect, and which carries the master's duties after a collision.
The COLREGs supply the standard of conduct. They do not themselves allocate loss; breach of them is the usual way in which fault is established.

blocks.p: One principle governs the whole subject: liability in collision is FAULT-BASED, not strict. If the collision is accidental, or is caused by force majeure, or if the cause of it is left in doubt on the evidence, the damages are borne by those who have suffered them - the loss lies where it falls. That is the baseline against which limbs (A), (B) and (D) all operate.

blocks.h: 2. (A) Apportionment of damages - the rule, and what it replaced

blocks.p: The rule. Where a collision is caused by the fault of two or more vessels, the liability of each vessel is in proportion to the degree of the fault respectively committed.

What it replaced, and why it is worth a line. Before the Convention, admiralty applied the rule of equal division: once both vessels were shown to be at fault to any extent at all, the loss was simply halved. A ship overwhelmingly to blame paid the same as one barely careless. The rule was easy to administer and plainly unjust, and the Convention's proportionate rule exists to replace it.

The fallback. The old rule survives only as a residue. Where the degrees of fault cannot be established from the evidence, or where the respective faults are equal, the liability is apportioned equally. So equal division is now the answer to an evidential failure, not the general rule.

blocks.h: 3. (A) How the shares are applied - and the split that matters most

blocks.p: Once the percentages are fixed, they are applied differently according to what was lost. This distinction carries most of the marks in limb (A).

rows: The vessels, their cargoes, and effects on board
Several - not joint. Each vessel answers only for her own proportion
A cargo owner must pursue both ships, and recovers only the relevant share from each. If one is insolvent or beyond reach, he bears that part of the loss
Loss of life and personal injury
Joint and several. Either vessel may be made to answer for the whole claim
The claimant sues whichever ship he can reach; that ship then has a right of recourse against the other for its proportion

blocks.p: The reason for the difference is a policy one and is worth stating: the law is content to make commercial parties chase their proportions between themselves, but it will not require a dead seafarer's family to sue two shipowners in two jurisdictions to be made whole.
Two practical points close the limb:

ul: Single liability or cross liabilities. In practice the claims are commonly settled on a single liability basis - the two claims are set against each other and only the net balance is paid. Marine policies may instead respond on a cross-liabilities basis, each claim being treated as paid in full, which can produce a different recovery for the assured.

The Both-to-Blame Collision Clause. Because cargo on the carrying ship can recover its share from the other vessel, and that vessel can pass part of that back to the carrying ship, the carrier ends up indirectly bearing a cargo liability from which the contract of carriage exempts him. The clause in the bill of lading requires the cargo owner to indemnify the carrier against that circularity.

blocks.h: 4. (B) Proportionate fault - what the degree actually measures

blocks.p: Fault here means a failure in the duty of good seamanship owed by each vessel to the other. In practice it is most often a breach of the COLREGs - a wrong or late alteration, an improper speed in restricted visibility, a failure to keep a proper lookout by sight, hearing and all available means, a failure to use radar and plotting properly - but it also covers negligent navigation generally, defective equipment, poor bridge or engine-room manning, and unseaworthiness.
The examinable proposition is what 'degree' measures, because it is not one thing but two:

ul: Blameworthiness - the culpability of the conduct. How far short of the standard of a prudent seaman did this ship fall? A deliberate or reckless breach weighs heavily; a momentary error of judgement in the agony of the moment weighs lightly, and may not be treated as fault at all where it was induced by the other ship's wrong.

Causative potency - how much the conduct actually contributed to the collision. A grave breach that made no difference to the outcome counts for little; a small lapse at exactly the decisive moment can carry the greater share.

blocks.p: Both are weighed together, and neither alone settles the share. A candidate who defines proportionate fault only as 'who was more to blame' has given half the answer.

blocks.h: 5. (B) How the degree is fixed, and where it cannot be

ul: The court assesses in broad percentages on the whole of the evidence - a judgement about the relative responsibility of the two ships, not an arithmetic. Apportionments are expressed in round terms, and no attempt at precision is made or expected.
Where more than two vessels are in fault, each bears her own proportion. A vessel not at fault bears nothing at all, whatever the others do between themselves.
Compulsory pilotage is no longer an answer. The presence of a compulsorily engaged pilot does not exonerate the ship from liability for negligent navigation.
Where the degrees cannot be established, the shares are equal - the fallback in section 2.
And where fault is not proved at all, there is no liability. Inevitable accident is a complete answer, not a mitigating factor.

blocks.h: 6. (C) Collision liabilities - the heads of claim

blocks.p: The phrase carries two questions - what may be claimed, and who finally bears it. Take them in that order.
Claims by and against the other vessel:

ul: Cost of repairs, together with drydocking, cleaning, gas-freeing, class and damage surveys;
Detention - loss of earnings or loss of hire while the ship is repaired, and the cost of any substitute tonnage;
Salvage rendered as a consequence of the collision, and any general average sacrifice or expenditure arising from it;
Total loss, where she is lost or is a constructive total loss.

blocks.p: Claims by others:

ul: Cargo on either ship, subject to the several / joint and several distinction in section 3;
Loss of life and personal injury - to crew, to passengers and to third parties;
Wreck removal and marking, which on a modern casualty is frequently the largest single head;
Damage to fixed and floating objects - berths, jetties, cranes, buoys, cables and aids to navigation;
Pure economic loss, which as a general rule is not recoverable in tort where it is unaccompanied by physical damage - the closed berth and the delayed third party usually recover nothing.

blocks.p: Pollution is a separate and stricter regime and must not be folded into the fault analysis. Where oil escapes, the oil pollution and bunkers conventions impose liability on the registered owner without proof of fault, channelled to him and backed by compulsory insurance with a right of direct action. So one casualty can generate a fault-based, apportioned claim between the ships and a strict-liability claim against one of them at the same time, and the two are answered by different rules.

blocks.h: 7. (C) Limitation, and where the liability finally lands

ul: Limitation. The shipowner may limit his aggregate liability for most collision claims by reference to the ship's tonnage, under the limitation convention, with separate funds for claims for loss of life and personal injury and for property claims. The right is lost where the loss resulted from his personal act or omission committed with intent to cause it, or recklessly and with knowledge that it would probably result. No limitation figure is quoted.

Hull and machinery insurance covers the ship's own damage, and through the collision liability clause - the running down clause - it covers three-fourths of the shipowner's liability to the other vessel, subject to the sum insured.

The P&I club carries the remaining one-fourth of the collision liability, and in addition the heads the hull policy does not touch at all: cargo, pollution, wreck removal, loss of life and personal injury, and damage to fixed and floating objects.

Time bar. Claims arising from a collision must be brought within two years of the casualty, with a further period for claims of contribution between the vessels. Preserving that limit by agreement or by issuing proceedings is a first step, not a last one.

blocks.h: 8. (D) Presumptions of fault - the abolition, and the one that survives

blocks.p: This limb has a counter-intuitive answer and that is why it is set.
The Convention abolished all legal presumptions of fault. Fault must be PROVED. The fact that a collision has occurred raises no presumption against either vessel.
What was abolished:

ul: the statutory presumption, formerly in English law and carried into the law of jurisdictions following it, that a ship found in breach of the collision regulations was deemed to have caused the collision unless she proved that the breach could not have contributed;
the presumptions once attaching to a vessel under way as against one at anchor or moored, and the various presumptions of the older admiralty practice.

blocks.p: What survives, and the distinction matters:

ul: Evidential inferences of fact. A vessel under way which strikes a properly anchored or moored vessel plainly calls for an explanation, and in the absence of one the court will readily find her at fault. That is an inference drawn from the evidence, not a rule of law that shifts the legal burden, and it is available to the tribunal in the ordinary way.
Breach of the COLREGs remains powerful evidence of fault - and is very often decisive. What it no longer does is prove causation automatically.

One genuine statutory presumption survives, and it is about conduct AFTER the collision. The master's duty is to stand by, render assistance to the other vessel and to those on board, and to exchange the identifying particulars of his ship. Where he fails in that duty without reasonable cause, the collision is presumed to have been caused by his wrongful act, neglect or default unless the contrary is shown - quite apart from the offence he commits by failing.

The important contrast: the United States is not a party to the Convention and retains the Pennsylvania Rule, under which a vessel shown to be in breach of a statutory rule intended to prevent collisions bears the burden of proving that her breach could not have been a cause. That is the direct opposite of the Convention position and is not the Indian position. Knowing the difference, and saying which applies, is what distinguishes a good answer here.

blocks.h: 9. How the four fit together in a single claim

blocks.p: The four limbs are one process, and the paper prints them in almost the reverse of the order a court works in:

ul: First (D) - was anyone at fault? Nothing is presumed; it must be proved.
Then (B) - how much fault, weighing blameworthiness against causative potency.
Then (A) - apply the shares: severally for property, jointly and severally for life and injury.
Then (C) - to what? The heads of claim, subject to limitation, and landing between hull underwriters and the club.

blocks.p: The abolition of presumptions is what makes the rest of it work. Apportioning a loss by degree is only a meaningful exercise if fault has been established on evidence rather than assumed from the fact of contact. That is also why the engineering evidence matters: the movement book, the voyage data recorder, the alarm and event printouts, the machinery and steering-gear logs and the maintenance records are the material from which a DEGREE - and not merely a fact - is afterwards established. Preserving them is a real duty on a Chief Engineer after a collision, and it is the point at which this doctrine touches his own job.

Four terms at four marks each, answered in the printed order, with two sections each on (A), (B) and (C) because each of those contains a rule plus the qualification that carries the mark. The framing section costs three lines and lets every limb afterwards refer to 'the Convention' without re-explaining it.

The closing section is where the marks above a bare pass are found. It shows that the candidate sees the four as one process, and it takes six lines. The link at the end to the engineering evidence is worth making in an oral even if it is cut in the written paper.

ul: Saying that breach of the COLREGs raises a presumption of fault. It is powerful evidence and it is not a presumption. This is the biggest single error available on this question.
Applying the Pennsylvania Rule as though it were the general law. It is United States law and the United States is not a party to the Convention.
Making all collision liability joint and several, or all of it several. Property is several; loss of life and personal injury is joint and several.
Defining proportionate fault as blameworthiness alone. Causative potency is the other half.
Writing an essay on limitation of liability under limb (C). It is one bullet of a four-mark limb.
Treating pollution as part of the apportionment. It is a strict-liability regime running alongside, not inside, the fault analysis.
Forgetting that equal division survives as the fallback where degrees cannot be established.
'The damage lies where it falls' - inevitable accident, force majeure or an unproved cause produce NO liability. Candidates instinctively look for someone to pay.
Compulsory pilotage is not a defence. The old exoneration is gone.
The surviving statutory presumption is about failing to stand by, which is conduct after the collision - not about the navigation that caused it.

Cargo cannot recover its whole loss from the other ship. Several liability means it recovers only that ship's proportion, which is exactly the circularity the Both-to-Blame Collision Clause addresses.
Pure economic loss is generally irrecoverable. The berth that lost a week's business usually gets nothing.
Three-fourths, not all, of the collision liability sits on the hull policy. The last quarter is the club's, and so is everything else.
Two years is the collision time bar, not the general commercial period.
Both ships are at fault and one sinks with her owner insolvent. Who bears the cargo loss?
Why is loss of life treated differently from cargo?
Your ship breached the steering and sailing rules but the other ship never saw you. How does that affect the apportionment?
What is the difference between single liability and cross liabilities, and who cares?
A collision in United States waters - does the analysis change?
What do you, as Chief Engineer, do in the first hour after a collision to protect the owner's position?
Can a shipowner always limit his liability?

blocks.p: Answer the four in the order a court actually works, and the whole subject becomes one sequence:

ul: Was anyone at fault? - nothing is presumed, it must be proved (limb D).
How much? - blameworthiness times causative potency (limb B).
How is it split? - property severally, life and injury jointly and severally (limb A).
Over what? - the heads of claim, then limitation, then hull three-quarters and club the rest (limb C).

blocks.p: Two sentences carry most of the marks: 'proportion to the degree of fault, replacing equal division', and 'the Convention abolished all legal presumptions of fault'.

rows: Collision Convention 1910
The source of the doctrine. Unamended. Proportionate liability; the equal-division fallback; the property / personal-injury split; the abolition of legal presumptions; the two-year time bar
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958
The Indian statute giving effect to those rules, and carrying the master's duty to stand by and the presumption that follows a failure to do so. No section cited
COLREGs 1972
The standard of conduct. Breach is evidence of fault, not a presumption of causation
Limitation convention (LLMC)
Tonnage-based limitation, separate funds for personal and property claims, and the conduct barring limitation. No figure quoted
Oil pollution and bunkers conventions
The strict, channelled liability that runs alongside the fault analysis where oil escapes
Collision liability (running down) clause
Hull cover for three-fourths of the liability to the other vessel
Both-to-Blame Collision Clause
The contractual answer to the cargo circularity created by several liability
The Pennsylvania Rule
United States law only. Named as the contrast; expressly not the Indian position

blocks.p: Neither governing instrument is held by the True Source corpus at 319524c. The Collision Convention of 1910 does not appear in the corpus's liability-and-compensation family, which covers HNS, Nairobi, the LLMC and the CLC/FUND/Bunkers group. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is not held either - the corpus holds the 2025 Act, which is future by roughly thirty-two months at this sitting. Every doctrinal proposition above is therefore authoritative secondary, given by identity and effect. No article is quoted and no section of the Indian Act is cited by number.

The jurisdictional caution is the important one on this question. The doctrine stated here is the Convention position as applied in India. The Pennsylvania Rule is stated only as a contrast and is expressly identified as United States law; a candidate who meets it in a textbook and applies it in an Indian paper will produce a confidently wrong answer to limb (D).

Two things are deliberately given without figures. The limitation amounts under the limitation convention are tonnage-based and have been revised; no figure is quoted. And the apportionment percentages courts award are illustrative of a practice, not a rule; no worked example is offered as though it were authority.

The surviving statutory presumption following a failure to stand by is stated at the level of effect. It exists in the Indian and English statutory scheme in materially the same terms, but the provision creating it was not read against primary text for this sitting, so no section is asserted.

questions.recurrence_adjudication: No recurrence in the 315-question set. This is the only question in the corpus that asks about collision as a matter of DOCTRINE - how fault is divided and what follows from the division - rather than as a casualty to be managed or a jurisdiction to be identified. Recorded as FRESH on a searched nil, with the six rejected collision questions named so that a reviewer can see the search was real.

blocks.p: Two ships hit each other. Almost always both of them did something wrong - one turned late, the other was going too fast, neither was really watching - and the whole of this question is about what the law does with that awkward fact.

The old answer was crude and it is worth knowing, because everything modern is a reaction to it. If both ships were to blame at all, the courts simply split the loss down the middle. It did not matter that one ship had been grossly negligent and the other barely careless; half each. That was easy to administer and obviously unjust, so the international rule was changed to say: each ship pays according to how much of the accident was really hers. If she was three-quarters to blame, she bears three-quarters.

Two refinements follow, and they are what the middle limbs are about. First, 'how much to blame' is not a single idea. A court weighs both how badly a ship behaved and how much that behaviour actually caused the collision - a serious rule breach that made no difference counts for less than a small lapse at exactly the wrong moment. Second, once the shares are fixed, they are applied differently depending on what was lost: for damaged property each ship answers only for her own share, so a cargo owner has to chase both ships; but where people are killed or hurt, either ship can be made to pay the whole claim and then go and recover from the other. The law will not make a widow chase two shipowners.

And the last limb is a piece of history that is still examined because the answer is counter-intuitive. There used to be rules saying that if you broke a navigation regulation you were assumed to have caused the collision unless you could prove otherwise. Those were swept away. Fault now has to be proved, not presumed - the fact of a collision proves nothing by itself. One narrow exception survives, and it is about running away afterwards rather than about the collision itself.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Four doctrinal terms from the law of collision, four marks each. The examiner is testing whether the candidate holds the DOCTRINE and not merely the practice. The four are not independent: (B) produces the shares, (A) applies them, (C) says what they are applied to, and (D) says what has to be proved before any of it starts. An answer that treats them as four unrelated definitions will be correct and will not score well. The single most examinable proposition on the whole question is that LEGAL PRESUMPTIONS OF FAULT WERE ABOLISHED - candidates habitually assert the opposite, because it feels as though breaking a rule of the road ought to prove something.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16, printed against each of (A) to (D). Two route sections are given to each of (A), (B) and (C) because each contains a rule and a qualification that carries the mark, and one to (D) plus a closing synthesis. Nothing may run long: the temptation on this question is to write an essay on limitation of liability under limb (C), which is worth at most a line or two of the four.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate names the Collision Convention of 1910 as the source of the proportionate rule and knows what it replaced. That 'degree of fault' is understood to combine BLAMEWORTHINESS and CAUSATIVE POTENCY rather than either alone. That the property/personal-injury split - several liability for property, JOINT AND SEVERAL for loss of life and personal injury - is stated, because it is the single most practically consequential rule in limb (A). That limb (D) is answered with the ABOLITION of presumptions and not with a list of them.
decomposition_gate.primary_source_plan: NEITHER GOVERNING INSTRUMENT IS HELD BY THE TRUE SOURCE CORPUS AT 319524c. The Collision Convention 1910 does not appear in the liability-and-compensation family, which covers HNS, Nairobi, LLMC and the CLC/FUND/Bunkers group; and the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is not held, the corpus holding the 2025 Act instead. Every doctrinal proposition is therefore AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY, given by article identity and effect with NOTHING QUOTED and no section of the Indian Act cited by number. The insurance tail in section 7 is carried from two MIW answers whose printed stems were read.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW - this is settled doctrine on a treaty of 1910 that has not been amended, applied through an Indian statute of 1958 that governed throughout this sitting. Nothing in the four limbs moved in the decade around July 2023. The only currency surfaces are the LLMC limitation figures, which are NOT quoted, and the Merchant Shipping Act 2025, which is future by roughly thirty-two months and does not appear.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: MEDIUM-HIGH, and it is the real risk on this question. The doctrine is international but its application is jurisdictional, and one important divergence must be handled: THE UNITED STATES IS NOT A PARTY TO THE 1910 CONVENTION AND RETAINS THE PENNSYLVANIA RULE, under which a ship in breach of a statutory rule bears the burden of showing her fault could not have contributed. That is the exact opposite of the Convention position and is the likeliest source of a confidently wrong answer. It is stated as a CONTRAST and expressly identified as not the Indian position.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: 'Collision liabilities' in limb (C) is ambiguous between the heads of claim and the incidence of the liability once apportioned. Both are given, in that order, because a candidate who gives only one has answered half the limb. 'Presumptions of fault' in limb (D) is likewise ambiguous between legal presumptions and evidential inferences; the answer distinguishes them, because res ipsa loquitur is an inference of fact and survives, while the legal presumptions do not.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Nine numbered sections with NO limb headings - the printed limb references are (A) to (D) in capitals, which the house heading convention does not admit, so the limb is carried in each section title instead. One framing section, two each for (A), (B) and (C), one for (D), and a closing synthesis running the four limbs through a single claim.

steps.title: The legal frame - which instruments govern a collision claim
points: The Collision Convention of 1910 - the Brussels convention unifying certain rules on collisions between vessels - is the source of the modern doctrine and is UNAMENDED
India gives it effect through the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958; the COLREGs supply the standard of conduct whose breach is the usual fault
Liability in collision is FAULT-BASED, not strict; where the collision is accidental, due to force majeure or its cause is left in doubt, THE DAMAGE LIES WHERE IT FALLS

steps.title: (A) Apportionment of damages - the rule, and what it replaced
points: THE RULE: where two or more vessels are in fault, liability is in PROPORTION TO THE DEGREE OF FAULT of each
WHAT IT REPLACED: the old admiralty rule of EQUAL DIVISION, under which any shared blame produced a half-and-half split regardless of degree
THE FALLBACK: where the degrees cannot be established, or the faults are equal, liability is apportioned EQUALLY - so equal division survives only as a residue

steps.title: (A) How the shares are applied - and the split that matters most
points: FOR PROPERTY - the vessels, their cargoes and the effects on board - liability is SEVERAL AND NOT JOINT. Each vessel answers only for her own share, so a cargo owner must pursue both ships
FOR LOSS OF LIFE AND PERSONAL INJURY - liability is JOINT AND SEVERAL. Either vessel may be made to pay the whole, with a right of recourse against the other for its share

IN PRACTICE the claims are usually settled on a SINGLE LIABILITY basis - the net balance is paid - although a policy may respond on CROSS LIABILITIES. The Both-to-Blame Collision Clause in a bill of lading is the contractual answer to the cargo consequence

steps.title: (B) Proportionate fault - what the degree actually measures
points: Fault means a failure in the duty of good seamanship - most often a breach of the COLREGs, but also bad lookout, excessive speed, defective equipment or an unseaworthy ship
THE DEGREE COMBINES TWO THINGS, AND THIS IS THE MARK: the BLAMEWORTHINESS of the conduct, and its CAUSATIVE POTENCY - how much it actually contributed
So a grave breach that made no difference weighs less than a small lapse at the decisive moment. Neither factor alone settles the share

steps.title: (B) How the degree is fixed, and where it cannot be
points: The court assesses in BROAD PERCENTAGES on the whole of the evidence - a range, not an arithmetic; no attempt at precision is made
More than two vessels: each bears its own proportion. A vessel not in fault bears nothing, whatever the others do
Where the degrees cannot be established the shares are EQUAL; and where fault is not proved at all there is no liability - INEVITABLE ACCIDENT is a complete answer, not a mitigation

steps.title: (C) Collision liabilities - the heads of claim
points: To the other ship: repairs, drydocking and survey, and the DETENTION or loss of hire while she is repaired; salvage and general average arising from the casualty
To others: cargo on both ships, LOSS OF LIFE AND PERSONAL INJURY, wreck removal and marking, and damage to fixed and floating objects such as berths, buoys and aids to navigation

POLLUTION IS A SEPARATE AND STRICTER REGIME - the oil pollution and bunkers conventions impose liability on the owner without proof of fault, so a collision can produce a fault-based claim and a strict-liability claim side by side. Pure economic loss is generally NOT recoverable

steps.title: (C) Limitation, and where the liability finally lands
points: The shipowner may LIMIT his liability by tonnage under the limitation convention, with separate funds for personal claims and property claims, unless the loss resulted from his personal act or omission committed with intent or recklessly with knowledge
HULL AND MACHINERY carries the ship's own damage and, through the COLLISION LIABILITY - RUNNING DOWN - CLAUSE, THREE QUARTERS of the liability to the other vessel

THE REMAINING QUARTER, and cargo, pollution, wreck removal, personal injury and damage to fixed and floating objects, fall to the P&I CLUB. Claims are time-barred after two years, with a further year for contribution

steps.title: (D) Presumptions of fault - the abolition, and the one that survives
points: THE HEADLINE: THE CONVENTION ABOLISHED ALL LEGAL PRESUMPTIONS OF FAULT. Fault must be PROVED; the fact of a collision proves nothing against either ship
What was abolished: the statutory presumption that a ship breaching the collision regulations caused the collision, and the presumptions attaching to a ship under way against one at anchor or moored

WHAT SURVIVES: an EVIDENTIAL inference of fact - a moving ship striking a properly moored one calls for an explanation - which is not a legal presumption; and the STATUTORY PRESUMPTION AGAINST A MASTER WHO FAILS IN HIS DUTY TO STAND BY and render assistance. CONTRAST: the United States is not a party and retains the Pennsylvania Rule, which reverses the burden - that is NOT the Indian position

steps.title: How the four fit together in a single claim
points: ORDER OF OPERATIONS: prove fault (D), measure its degree (B), apply the shares (A), to the heads of claim (C)
The abolition of presumptions is what makes the rest work - proportion is only meaningful if fault has been established rather than assumed
And it explains the evidence a Chief Engineer is asked for: the movement book, the data recorder, the alarm printout and the machinery logs are how a DEGREE, not merely a fact, is later established

questions.memory_cue: Four questions in the order a court answers them: WAS ANYONE AT FAULT (8), HOW MUCH (4-5), HOW IS IT SPLIT (2-3), OVER WHAT (6-7). Reversed by the paper, joined again at (9).

quick_revision.recall_15s: LIABILITY IN COLLISION IS FAULT-BASED, NOT STRICT. If the collision is accidental, due to force majeure, or its cause is left in doubt, THE DAMAGE LIES WHERE IT FALLS. Source: the COLLISION CONVENTION OF 1910, unamended, given effect in India through the MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT 1958; the COLREGs supply the standard of conduct. (A) APPORTIONMENT - where two or more vessels are in fault, liability is IN PROPORTION TO THE DEGREE OF FAULT of each. This REPLACED THE OLD RULE OF EQUAL DIVISION, which halved the loss whatever the degrees. FALLBACK: where the degrees cannot be established, or the faults are equal, liability is APPORTIONED EQUALLY. APPLICATION - for the vessels, their cargoes and effects, liability is SEVERAL AND NOT JOINT, so cargo must pursue both ships; for LOSS OF LIFE AND PERSONAL INJURY it is JOINT AND SEVERAL, with a right of recourse. Settled in practice on SINGLE LIABILITY, though a policy may respond on CROSS LIABILITIES; the BOTH-TO-BLAME COLLISION CLAUSE answers the cargo circularity. (B) PROPORTIONATE FAULT - fault is a failure in good seamanship, usually a COLREG breach but also lookout, speed, equipment or unseaworthiness. THE DEGREE COMBINES BLAMEWORTHINESS AND CAUSATIVE POTENCY - a grave breach that made no difference weighs less than a small lapse at the decisive moment. Assessed in BROAD PERCENTAGES on the whole evidence; each of several vessels bears her own proportion; COMPULSORY PILOTAGE IS NO DEFENCE; INEVITABLE ACCIDENT IS A COMPLETE ANSWER. (C) LIABILITIES - repairs, drydocking and survey, DETENTION and loss of hire, salvage, general average, total loss; cargo on both ships; LOSS OF LIFE AND PERSONAL INJURY; WRECK REMOVAL AND MARKING; damage to FIXED AND FLOATING OBJECTS; PURE ECONOMIC LOSS GENERALLY NOT RECOVERABLE. POLLUTION IS A SEPARATE STRICT REGIME running alongside. Owner may LIMIT BY TONNAGE with separate funds for personal and property claims, losing the right on his personal act or omission with intent or recklessly with knowledge. HULL AND MACHINERY carries THREE-FOURTHS of the liability to the other vessel through the RUNNING DOWN CLAUSE; the REMAINING QUARTER and cargo, pollution, wreck removal, injury and fixed and floating objects fall to the P&I CLUB. TIME BAR TWO YEARS. (D) PRESUMPTIONS - THE CONVENTION ABOLISHED ALL LEGAL PRESUMPTIONS OF FAULT; FAULT MUST BE PROVED and the fact of a collision proves nothing. Abolished: the statutory presumption from breach of the collision regulations, and the presumptions attaching to a ship under way against one moored. SURVIVING: EVIDENTIAL INFERENCES of fact, which are not legal presumptions; and the STATUTORY PRESUMPTION AGAINST A MASTER WHO FAILS TO STAND BY. CONTRAST: the UNITED STATES is not a party and retains the PENNSYLVANIA RULE, which reverses the burden - NOT the Indian position.
keywords: proportion to the degree of fault
critical_numbers: Liability apportioned in PROPORTION to the degree of fault - equal only where degrees cannot be established or faults are equal
THREE-FOURTHS of the collision liability to the other vessel sits on the hull policy; the remaining quarter on the P&I club
Collision claims time-barred after TWO YEARS, with a further period for contribution
Four printed limbs at 4 marks each
quick_revision.critical_regulation: The Collision Convention of 1910 - proportionate liability by degree of fault, equal apportionment where the degrees cannot be established, several liability for property and joint and several liability for loss of life and personal injury, and the ABOLITION OF ALL LEGAL PRESUMPTIONS OF FAULT. Given effect in India through the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
quick_revision.major_trap: Asserting that breach of the COLREGs raises a PRESUMPTION of fault or of causation. It does not - the Convention abolished all legal presumptions of fault, and a breach is powerful EVIDENCE that must still be shown to have contributed. The related trap is importing the PENNSYLVANIA RULE, under which the burden shifts to the ship in breach: that is United States law, the United States is not a party to the Convention, and it is the direct opposite of the position that governs an Indian sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the rule on apportionment of damages in collision, and say what it replaced.
retrieval_cards.answer: Where a collision is caused by the fault of two or more vessels, the liability of each is IN PROPORTION TO THE DEGREE OF FAULT respectively committed. It replaced the old admiralty rule of EQUAL DIVISION, under which any shared fault halved the loss regardless of degree. Equal division now survives only as the fallback where the degrees cannot be established or the faults are equal.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is collision liability joint and several, or several?
retrieval_cards.answer: Both, according to what was lost. For the vessels, their cargoes and effects on board it is SEVERAL AND NOT JOINT - each vessel answers only for her own proportion, so a cargo owner must pursue both ships. For LOSS OF LIFE AND PERSONAL INJURY it is JOINT AND SEVERAL - either vessel may be made to pay the whole, with a right of recourse against the other for its share.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What two things does 'degree of fault' measure?
retrieval_cards.answer: BLAMEWORTHINESS - how far the conduct fell short of the standard of a prudent seaman; and CAUSATIVE POTENCY - how much that conduct actually contributed to the collision. Both are weighed together. A grave breach that made no difference weighs less than a small lapse at the decisive moment, and neither factor alone settles the share.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does a breach of the COLREGs raise a presumption that the breaching ship caused the collision?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The Collision Convention of 1910 ABOLISHED ALL LEGAL PRESUMPTIONS OF FAULT; fault must be proved and the fact of a collision raises no presumption against either vessel. A COLREG breach is powerful evidence of fault, often decisive, but causation must still be established. The old statutory presumption to the contrary was swept away.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the Pennsylvania Rule, and does it apply to an Indian collision claim?
retrieval_cards.answer: A rule of United States law under which a vessel shown to be in breach of a statutory rule intended to prevent collisions bears the burden of proving that her breach COULD NOT HAVE BEEN a cause of the collision. It is the direct opposite of the Convention position. The United States is not a party to the 1910 Convention, and the rule is NOT the Indian position.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does a collision liability finally land, as between hull underwriters and the P&I club?
retrieval_cards.answer: Hull and machinery covers the ship's own damage and, through the collision liability or running down clause, THREE-FOURTHS of the liability to the other vessel. The remaining ONE-FOURTH falls to the P&I club, together with the heads the hull policy does not touch at all: cargo, pollution, wreck removal, loss of life and personal injury, and damage to fixed and floating objects.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Both ships are damaged but neither fault can be proved. Who pays?
retrieval_cards.answer: Nobody. Liability in collision is fault-based. Where the collision is accidental, caused by force majeure, or its cause is left in doubt on the evidence, the damages are borne by those who have suffered them - the damage lies where it falls. Inevitable accident is a complete answer, not a mitigation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which presumption of fault survives the Convention, and what triggers it?
retrieval_cards.answer: The statutory presumption attaching to a failure to STAND BY. The master must stand by, render assistance to the other vessel and those on board, and exchange his ship's identifying particulars. Where he fails without reasonable cause, the collision is presumed to have been caused by his wrongful act, neglect or default unless the contrary is shown - and separately he commits an offence. Note it concerns conduct AFTER the collision, not the navigation that caused it.

notes: THE GOVERNING INSTRUMENT IS UNAMENDED AND MORE THAN A CENTURY OLD. The Collision Convention of 1910 carries no amendment, so there is no edition question and no entry-into-force boundary anywhere near this sitting. The doctrine stated here would be stated the same way for a sitting ten years either side.

THE INDIAN STATUTE IS RESOLVED AND IS THE STANDING BATCH TRAP. The MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, 1958 governs throughout this sitting. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026, roughly THIRTY-TWO MONTHS after this paper, and appears nowhere. The administration at this sitting is DG Shipping; the renamed body does not appear.

NO DONOR EXISTS, SO THERE IS NO DONOR CONTAMINATION SURFACE ON THE DOCTRINE. Six collision questions were read and rejected with reasons recorded. TWO LATER QUESTIONS WERE PARTIALLY CONSUMED FOR THE INSURANCE TAIL ONLY - QP2407-Q8 (July 2024) and QP2411-Q6 (November 2024), both twelve to sixteen months later. They were read in full and searched for sitting-relative prose and later law; the three-fourths collision liability clause and the P&I / hull division are market practice of long standing and carry no date, and NOTHING ELSE WAS TAKEN.
THE 7 JULY 2023 GHG BOUNDARY DOES NOT ENGAGE THIS QUESTION. It is private maritime law; no IMO greenhouse gas measure bears on any of the four limbs. Assessed and clear.

THE REAL RISK ON THIS QUESTION IS JURISDICTIONAL RATHER THAN TEMPORAL, AND IT HAS BEEN HANDLED EXPRESSLY. The Pennsylvania Rule survives in the United States, which is not a party to the 1910 Convention, and it REVERSES the burden the Convention removed. It is stated only as a contrast and is expressly identified as not the Indian position, because a candidate who meets it in a general textbook and applies it here produces a confidently wrong answer to limb (D).

NO LIMITATION FIGURE IS QUOTED. The limitation convention's amounts are tonnage-based and have been revised more than once; quoting a figure would be a currency exposure the question does not require, and the corpus records those values as verify-before-citing.
NO APPORTIONMENT PERCENTAGE IS OFFERED AS AUTHORITY. Courts award in broad percentages and the practice is described; no worked example is presented as though it were a rule.

FUTURE CONTAMINATION SWEEP, RUN AND CLEAN. The 33rd Assembly adopted on 6 December 2023, five months after this sitting, and no A.11xx(33) instrument appears. The Hong Kong Convention, in force 26 June 2025, does not appear notwithstanding that wreck removal is one of the heads of claim. The Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention is not asserted to apply to any particular State at any particular date.

regulations: Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules of Law with respect to Collisions between Vessels, Brussels 1910 (the Collision Convention) - the source of the doctrine; UNAMENDED. Proportionate liability by degree of fault; equal apportionment where the degrees cannot be established or the faults are equal; several liability for the vessels, cargoes and effects, and joint and several liability for loss of life and personal injury; the abolition of all legal presumptions of fault; and the two-year time bar

Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (India) - the statute giving effect to those rules at this sitting, and carrying the master's duty to stand by and render assistance after a collision, together with the presumption that follows a failure to do so. NO SECTION IS CITED BY NUMBER
COLREGs 1972 - the standard of conduct whose breach is the usual foundation of fault. Evidence of fault; NOT a presumption of causation

Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims (LLMC) - tonnage-based limitation, separate funds for claims for loss of life and personal injury and for property claims, and the conduct barring limitation. Identity level; NO FIGURE QUOTED
Civil Liability Convention 1992 and the Bunkers Convention 2001 - the strict, channelled pollution liability that runs alongside the fault-based collision claim. Named by identity and effect only
The collision liability (running down) clause in hull and machinery insurance - three-fourths of the liability to the other vessel. Commercial contract, not an instrument
The Both-to-Blame Collision Clause in bills of lading - the contractual answer to the cargo circularity created by several liability. Commercial contract, not an instrument
THE PENNSYLVANIA RULE - UNITED STATES LAW ONLY. Named as a contrast and expressly excluded as the applicable position

cross_links.label: QP2307 Q2 - risk assessment as it is actually done on a ship, which FSA is deliberately not

blocks.h: 1. What FSA is, and its objectives

blocks.p: Formal Safety Assessment is a structured and systematic methodology aimed at enhancing maritime safety - including protection of life, health, the marine environment and property - by using risk analysis and cost-benefit assessment. It is set out in the Revised Guidelines for Formal Safety Assessment for use in the IMO rule-making process, MSC-MEPC.2/Circ.12/Rev.2, issued 9 April 2018 - five years before this sitting and unrevised since.

Say what kind of thing it is before anything else, because the whole answer follows from it: FSA is a tool for making RULES, not for running a ship. The Company's obligation under the ISM Code to assess risks to its ships and personnel and to establish safeguards is a different exercise - a different body, a different scale, a different output. Confusing the two is the framing error on this question.
Its objectives are:

ul: to provide a rational and systematic process for assessing the risks associated with shipping activity, and for evaluating the costs and benefits of options for reducing those risks;
to provide a means of evaluating new regulations, or of comparing existing regulations with proposed ones, so that safety and environmental benefit can be weighed against cost;
to assist in demonstrating to decision-makers that a proposed measure delivers a benefit in proportion to what it costs;
to support equitable and consistent regulatory change, and to aid the reaching of consensus among Member States by making the reasoning visible rather than assertive.

blocks.p: One honest qualification belongs here: the Guidelines do not claim that FSA is applied in all circumstances. It is a tool for the questions that need it, not a mandatory precondition for every amendment.

ul: Proactive, not reactive. It argues about a rule before the rule exists, rather than after a casualty. This is the single most important characteristic and belongs first.
Structured and systematic, so that two studies of the same problem can be compared and the reasoning followed.
Transparent, documented and auditable - every assumption, data source and judgement is recorded, because the output is meant to persuade a committee of States rather than to satisfy its own author.
Generic rather than ship-specific. It is applied to a generic model of a ship type, system or operation, not to one vessel. That is what makes the result usable as a rule.
Proportionate in depth. The work is screened so that effort goes where the risk is, instead of being spread uniformly.
Iterative. The steps are not a one-way corridor - findings at a later step send you back to an earlier one, and step 5 draws on all of them.
Explicitly cost-aware. Alone among the safety methods in common use, it requires the cost of a proposed measure to be estimated and compared with the risk it removes.

blocks.h: 3. The process - and the step that is not one of the five

blocks.p: Before step 1, the decision-makers define the problem: the ship type, system or operation to be studied, the scope and boundaries, the operating conditions assumed, and the regulations already in force. This is preparatory and it is NOT one of the five steps. Calling it step 1 and pushing hazard identification to step 2 is the commonest structural error on this question.
Two definitions are needed before going further:

ul: a hazard is a potential to threaten human life, health, property or the environment;
risk is the combination of the frequency of an occurrence and the severity of its consequence.

blocks.p: The five steps are then:

rows: Hazard Identification
What could go wrong?
Risk Analysis
How likely is it, and how bad?
Risk Control Options
What could be done about it?
Cost Benefit Assessment
What would that cost, against what it saves?
Recommendations for decision-making
What should therefore be required?

blocks.p: Purpose: to produce a prioritised list of hazards and of the accident scenarios they lead to, specific to the problem defined.

ul: The creative element - a structured group review by a balanced team of people with practical experience: seagoing officers, designers, operators, surveyors and risk specialists, using techniques such as structured what-if and hazard and operability review. Its purpose is to find hazards that the data do not contain because they have not happened yet.

The analytical element - casualty and incident data, port State control and class defect records, published studies and previous FSA work. Its purpose is to make sure the known hazards are not overlooked while the group is being imaginative.
Both are necessary. Data alone will miss the novel hazard; imagination alone will miss the common one. A candidate who gives only one of the two has given half the step.
A coarse analysis of causes and consequences is carried out for each hazard, sufficient only to rank it - not to analyse it, which is step 2's job.

Ranking on a risk matrix of frequency against severity, so that the small number of scenarios carrying most of the risk are carried into step 2 and the remainder are screened out. This is where the proportionality characteristic is actually applied.
Output: a ranked list of hazards and scenarios, with the initiating events and the accident categories they belong to.

blocks.p: Purpose: to examine in detail the causes and consequences of the scenarios carried forward from step 1, and to quantify the risk so that contributors can be compared with one another.

ul: Fault tree analysis works backwards from an undesired event to the combinations of failures and conditions that could produce it, and yields an estimate of its frequency.
Event tree analysis works forwards from an initiating event, through each barrier or intervention that may or may not succeed, and yields the spread of consequences and their probabilities.
Together they form the risk contribution tree - causes on one side, consequences on the other, the accident event in the middle. That structure is the whole of step 2 in one picture.

Results are expressed as individual risk - the risk to a particular person, typically a crew member - and as societal risk, the risk to the whole exposed population, commonly presented on an FN curve plotting frequency against number of fatalities.

The results are judged against the ALARP framework: a region of risk that is intolerable and must be reduced whatever the cost; a middle region that is tolerable only if the risk is as low as reasonably practicable, where cost may properly be weighed; and a region so small as to be broadly acceptable. The middle region is where step 4 does its work.

The output that matters is not a single number but which contributors dominate - which causes and which consequences carry most of the risk - because those are the only places a control option can usefully be aimed.

blocks.p: Purpose: to devise measures that reduce the dominant contributors identified in step 2, and to assemble them into options a regulator could actually adopt.

ul: Individual risk control measures are generated against the dominant contributors, and are classified two ways: whether they are preventive - reducing the frequency of the event - or mitigating, reducing its consequence; and whether they are engineering, procedural or organisational.

Measures sharing common risk-reducing attributes are then grouped into risk control OPTIONS. This is the step's distinctive move and it is regularly missed: a regulation is adopted as a coherent package, not as a single bolt or a single procedure, so the assessment must evaluate packages.
Each option is examined for practicability, cost, effectiveness and confidence - and for whether it introduces new hazards of its own, which is why the process is iterative.
The risk reduction attributable to each option is then re-evaluated through the step 2 model, giving the change in risk that step 4 will divide the cost by.
Output: a list of risk control options with the risk reduction each achieves.

blocks.p: Purpose: to determine the cost-effectiveness of each risk control option - what it costs set against the risk it removes.
The assessment is made over the whole life cycle and across the whole affected fleet, not for one ship in one year. That scope is what makes the result usable as a rule.

ul: Costs include design and construction, equipment and retrofit, installation and downtime, training, survey and certification, operating and maintenance cost, and any loss of earning capacity - lost deadweight, lost cargo space, lost speed.

Benefits include fatalities and injuries averted, casualties and pollution incidents avoided, property and cargo preserved, reduced insurance and clean-up cost, and any operational saving the measure itself produces.

blocks.p: These are then expressed as cost-effectiveness indices, and naming them is what turns a vague weighing into an answer:

ul: the gross cost of averting a fatality - the additional cost of the option divided by the reduction in risk it achieves, expressed per fatality averted;

the net cost of averting a fatality - the same calculation after subtracting the economic benefit the measure itself produces. Where a measure pays for itself in avoided loss, the net figure can be negative, which is the strongest possible case for adopting it.

blocks.p: The indices are compared against a criterion of what society is prepared to pay to avert a fatality, and are used to rank the options. No criterion value is quoted here: the figure is a matter for the decision-makers, is periodically revisited, and asserting one would be to state as fact something the Guidelines leave open.

Two honest qualifications close the step. The benefits are dominated by items that are genuinely hard to value, and the indices are sensitive to the assumptions behind them - which is why step 5 requires the assumptions to be exposed. And cost-effectiveness is a ranking tool, not a decision rule: a measure may be adopted although it is expensive, or rejected although it is cheap, for reasons the calculation does not contain.

blocks.h: 8. Step 5 - Recommendations, and what FSA does not settle

blocks.p: Purpose: to present decision-makers with ranked and justified recommendations drawn from steps 1 to 4.

ul: The recommendations set out which options are recommended, in what order, with the risk reduction and the cost-effectiveness of each.

The assumptions, the quality of the data and the uncertainties are exposed alongside them, not buried. A recommendation whose sensitivity to a doubtful assumption is hidden is worse than no recommendation.
Where the analysis cannot support a conclusion, that is itself reported.

The study is submitted to the relevant IMO Committee and is subject to independent expert review before it is relied on - which is the transparency characteristic made operational rather than merely asserted.

blocks.p: Close on the limits of the method, because an answer that presents FSA as a machine for producing correct rules has misunderstood it:

ul: FSA does not decide. It informs a judgement that remains with the Member States, and that judgement is properly political as well as technical.
FSA does not make a ship safe. It helps produce a better rule; the rule is then implemented, surveyed and lived with by people on ships.
FSA cannot be better than its data. Casualty data are incomplete and under-reported, and a generic model is by definition an abstraction from every real ship it covers.
And it is only as honest as its assumptions - which is precisely why transparency, documentation and independent review are not decoration but the conditions on which the method works at all.

blocks.p: The stem names five things - objectives, characteristics, processes, and then three of the five steps by name. The answer gives all five in the order asked, and the mark is secured by giving the whole process and then going deeper where directed, rather than answering only the three steps the examiner happened to list.

Section 3 is the load-bearing one. Separating 'define the problem' from the five steps, and defining hazard and risk before describing them, costs about six lines and prevents the structural error that most damages this answer.

ul: Calling 'define the problem' step 1. It is preparatory. There are five steps and hazard identification is the first of them.
Answering only the three named steps. The question asks for the objectives, characteristics and processes first, with specific explanation of three. Both parts are required.
Confusing FSA with ISM risk assessment. One makes rules; the other runs a ship.
Giving hazard identification as a data exercise only, or as a brainstorm only. It is both, and the reason both are needed is a mark in itself.
Describing cost-benefit assessment without naming the cost-effectiveness indices. The gross and net cost of averting a fatality are what make the step concrete.
Presenting FSA as deciding anything. It recommends; the Committee decides.
Forgetting that risk control MEASURES are grouped into risk control OPTIONS.
Risk is frequency AND severity. An answer that treats risk as probability alone cannot explain why a rare catastrophe is treated differently from a frequent nuisance.
ALARP has three regions, not two. The middle one is where cost may properly be weighed - and it is the only place step 4 is legitimate.
Fault tree backwards, event tree forwards. Candidates reverse them.
Preventive reduces frequency; mitigating reduces consequence. Simple, and regularly muddled.
Do not quote a figure for what society will pay to avert a fatality. It is periodically revisited and the Guidelines leave it to the decision-makers.
FSA is generic, not ship-specific. If the answer describes a study of one vessel, it has described the wrong thing.
The method is iterative. Step 3 can send you back to step 2, and a new hazard introduced by a control option goes back to step 1.
What is the difference between a hazard and a risk?
Why do you need a brainstorming session at all if you have twenty years of casualty data?
What does a negative net cost of averting a fatality mean, and does it settle the question?
Give me an example of a preventive measure and a mitigating measure for the same accident.
Where does ALARP come into it?
Who reviews an FSA study before IMO acts on it?
How is this different from the risk assessment your Company does under the ISM Code?

blocks.p: Define the problem first - but do not number it. Then five questions in order, each one a step:

ul: What could go wrong? - Hazard Identification.
How likely, and how bad? - Risk Analysis.
What could be done about it? - Risk Control Options.
What would that cost, against what it saves? - Cost Benefit Assessment.
What should therefore be required? - Recommendations for decision-making.

blocks.p: For the characteristics, one sentence carries most of them: proactive, generic, transparent, iterative, and explicitly cost-aware.

rows: The revised FSA Guidelines
The IMO methodology circular that defines the objectives, the characteristics and the five steps. Cited by identity; nothing quoted
ISM Code
Named only as the CONTRAST - the Company's own risk assessment, a different exercise at a different scale
The relevant IMO Committee
The body to which a study is submitted, and which decides. FSA informs; it does not decide
ALARP
The tolerability framework against which step 2's results are judged, and which makes step 4 legitimate in the middle region
GCAF and NCAF
The cost-effectiveness indices of step 4. No criterion value is quoted

blocks.p: The FSA Guidelines are not held by the True Source corpus at 319524c. No FSA circular appears anywhere in the corpus's IMO instruments holdings. The method above is therefore carried as verified internal reuse through two MIW answers to the character-identical stem, both read in full this session, supported by authoritative secondary knowledge of the Guidelines. The Guidelines are cited by identity and nothing is quoted.

No criterion value for the cost of averting a fatality is given. The figure is a matter for the decision-makers, is periodically revisited, and asserting one would state as settled something the Guidelines deliberately leave open. The indices themselves - gross and net - are described, which is what the question needs.

The list of characteristics is a synthesis, not a transcription. The Guidelines express these properties across the document rather than as a numbered list, so the seven given here are an organised statement of what the method is, and are declared as such rather than presented as a quoted enumeration.

One point of comfort on this question. Its printed stem recurs character-identically at December 2023 and at June 2026, and the MIW treatment of it is stable across those thirty-five months. That stability is itself evidence that the methodology described here did not move around this sitting.

This is one examiner question set three times across thirty-five months without a word changing. The only difference anywhere is that this sitting prints no mark figure where the other two print (16) - an absence, not a variation, and recorded as such. Classified EXACT.

blocks.p: For most of maritime history the rules were written after the funerals. Something terrible happened, an inquiry sat, and a requirement appeared to stop that exact thing happening again. It worked, in the sense that each rule was well aimed - but it meant the rulebook was a list of past disasters, and it could say nothing at all about a risk that had not yet killed anybody.

This is the method that was built to argue about a rule before the rule exists. Its logic is ordinary once stated. Take a type of ship or a way of operating. Ask what could go wrong, systematically rather than by memory. Work out, for each of those, how often it is likely to happen and how bad it would be when it does - because those two together are what people actually mean by risk, and a rare catastrophe and a frequent nuisance can need very different treatment. Then ask what could be done about the worst of them, and - this is the part that makes the method unusual - work out what each of those fixes would cost, and compare that with the harm it would prevent.

The cost step is not cynicism; it is the reason the method persuades anybody. A committee of governments and industries will not adopt a requirement simply because it is safer, because everything is safer if you spend enough. What moves them is being shown that a particular measure buys a particular amount of safety for a particular price, and that the reasoning is written down where anyone can attack it.

Two things follow that are worth carrying into the exam room. It studies a generic ship, not a real one - the output has to serve as a rule for a whole class of vessel, so it cannot be a study of one owner's problem. And it does not decide anything. It hands decision-makers a ranked set of options with the assumptions exposed. The deciding is still done by people in a committee room, which is exactly as it should be.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A single unlimbed question that nonetheless names five things and expects all five: the OBJECTIVES, the CHARACTERISTICS, the PROCESS, and then specific explanation of THREE of the five steps - hazard identification, risk analysis and cost benefit assessment. The examiner has named three steps and not the other two, which is a test of whether the candidate gives the whole process and then goes deeper where asked, rather than giving only the three named. The framing error the question is really testing is confusion between FSA and the risk assessment a Company does under the ISM Code: FSA is a tool for making RULES, not for running a ship.

Planned as: objectives and characteristics about a quarter of the answer, the process and its five steps about half with the three named steps carrying most of that, and the closing on what FSA does not settle the remainder. The two unnamed steps are given properly but briefly - omitting them would break the process, and expanding them would spend marks the examiner has directed elsewhere.

That risk is defined as the combination of frequency and severity before step 2 is described. The method is therefore carried as INTERNAL_REUSE_VERIFIED through QP2312-Q9 and QP2606-Q9, both read in full this session, supported by authoritative secondary knowledge of the Guidelines. steps.title: What FSA is, and its objectives
points: A STRUCTURED AND SYSTEMATIC METHODOLOGY for enhancing maritime safety - life, health, the marine environment and property - using RISK ANALYSIS and COST-BENEFIT ASSESSMENT
IT IS A TOOL FOR MAKING RULES, NOT FOR RUNNING A SHIP. The Company's ISM risk assessment is a different exercise by a different body at a different scale

Objectives: a rational and systematic process; a means of evaluating new regulations or comparing existing with proposed; assistance in demonstrating benefit proportionate to cost; and support for equitable, consistent regulatory change and consensus

steps.title: The characteristics that define it
points: PROACTIVE, NOT REACTIVE - it argues about a rule BEFORE the rule exists, instead of after a casualty. This belongs first
Structured and systematic; transparent, documented and auditable; GENERIC rather than ship-specific; proportionate in depth; iterative
EXPLICITLY COST-AWARE - alone among safety methods in common use it requires the cost of a measure to be estimated and compared with the risk it removes

steps.title: The process - and the step that is not one of the five
points: BEFORE step 1 the decision-makers DEFINE THE PROBLEM - ship type, system or operation, scope and boundaries, operating conditions, relevant regulations. THIS IS PREPARATORY AND IS NOT ONE OF THE FIVE STEPS

Two definitions are needed first: a HAZARD is a potential to threaten life, health, property or the environment; RISK is the combination of the FREQUENCY of an occurrence and the SEVERITY of its consequence
The five steps: Hazard Identification, Risk Analysis, Risk Control Options, Cost Benefit Assessment, Recommendations for decision-making

steps.title: Step 1 - Hazard Identification
points: Purpose: a PRIORITISED LIST of hazards and of the accident scenarios they lead to, specific to the problem defined

THE CREATIVE ELEMENT - a structured group review by a balanced team using structured what-if and hazard and operability techniques, to find hazards the data do not contain BECAUSE THEY HAVE NOT HAPPENED YET

THE ANALYTICAL ELEMENT - casualty and incident data, port State control and class defect records, previous studies. BOTH ARE NECESSARY: data alone misses the novel hazard, imagination alone misses the common one. Coarse analysis, then RANKING on a frequency-severity matrix so that effort goes where the risk is

steps.title: Step 2 - Risk Analysis
points: Purpose: to understand the CAUSES and CONSEQUENCES of the scenarios carried forward, and to quantify the risk so that it can be compared

FAULT TREES work backwards from an event to its causes and give FREQUENCY; EVENT TREES work forwards from an initiating event through the barriers and give the spread of CONSEQUENCES. Together they form the risk contribution tree

Results as INDIVIDUAL RISK and SOCIETAL RISK, the latter often on an FN curve; judged against ALARP - intolerable, tolerable if as low as reasonably practicable, or negligible. The output is WHICH CONTRIBUTORS DOMINATE, because that is where a control option can do work

steps.title: Step 3 - Risk Control Options
points: Purpose: to devise measures that reduce the dominant contributors, and to assemble them into practical options
Individual RISK CONTROL MEASURES are classified by whether they are PREVENTIVE (reduce frequency) or MITIGATING (reduce consequence), and by whether they are engineering, procedural or organisational

Measures with common risk-reducing attributes are GROUPED INTO RISK CONTROL OPTIONS, because a regulation is adopted as a package and not as a single bolt. Each option's risk reduction is then re-evaluated through step 2

steps.title: Step 4 - Cost Benefit Assessment
points: Purpose: to determine the cost-effectiveness of each option - what it costs against the risk it removes, over the LIFE CYCLE and across the whole affected fleet

COSTS: design, build, retrofit, equipment, training, survey, operation, maintenance, and any loss of earning capacity. BENEFITS: fatalities and injuries averted, casualties and pollution avoided, property and cargo preserved, and any operational saving

Expressed as COST-EFFECTIVENESS INDICES - the GROSS cost of averting a fatality, and the NET cost, which subtracts the economic benefit the measure itself produces. NO CRITERION VALUE IS QUOTED: the indices RANK options and inform a decision; they do not make it

steps.title: Step 5 - Recommendations, and what FSA does not settle
points: Purpose: to present decision-makers with RANKED, JUSTIFIED recommendations, with the assumptions, the data quality and the uncertainties exposed alongside them
The study is submitted to the relevant IMO Committee and is subject to independent expert review before it is relied on - the transparency characteristic made operational
WHAT FSA DOES NOT DO: it does not decide, it does not make a ship safe, and it cannot be better than its data. It informs a political and technical judgement that remains with the Member States

questions.memory_cue: Define the problem FIRST but do not number it (3). Then WHAT COULD GO WRONG (4), HOW LIKELY AND HOW BAD (5), WHAT COULD BE DONE (6), WHAT WOULD IT COST (7), WHAT SHOULD BE REQUIRED (8).

quick_revision.recall_15s: FSA IS A STRUCTURED AND SYSTEMATIC METHODOLOGY for enhancing maritime safety - life, health, the marine environment and property - USING RISK ANALYSIS AND COST-BENEFIT ASSESSMENT. IT IS A TOOL FOR MAKING RULES, NOT FOR RUNNING A SHIP - the ISM risk assessment is a different exercise. OBJECTIVES: a rational and systematic process for assessing risk and evaluating the cost and benefit of reducing it; a means of evaluating new regulations or comparing existing with proposed; assistance in demonstrating benefit proportionate to cost; and support for equitable, consistent change and for consensus. CHARACTERISTICS: PROACTIVE NOT REACTIVE; structured and systematic; transparent, documented and auditable; GENERIC not ship-specific; proportionate in depth; ITERATIVE; and EXPLICITLY COST-AWARE. BEFORE STEP 1 THE PROBLEM IS DEFINED - ship type, scope, boundaries, operating conditions, existing regulations - AND THIS IS NOT ONE OF THE FIVE STEPS. A HAZARD is a potential to threaten life, health, property or the environment; RISK is the combination of FREQUENCY and SEVERITY. FIVE STEPS: 1 HAZARD IDENTIFICATION - what could go wrong: a CREATIVE element (structured group review, what-if, hazard and operability) to find what has not happened yet, and an ANALYTICAL element (casualty, PSC and class data) to catch what has; coarse analysis then RANKING on a frequency-severity matrix. 2 RISK ANALYSIS - how likely and how bad: FAULT TREES BACKWARDS to causes giving frequency, EVENT TREES FORWARDS through barriers giving consequences, together the risk contribution tree; individual and SOCIETAL risk, FN curves, judged against ALARP - intolerable, tolerable if as low as reasonably practicable, or negligible; the output is WHICH CONTRIBUTORS DOMINATE. 3 RISK CONTROL OPTIONS - what could be done: measures classified PREVENTIVE (reduce frequency) or MITIGATING (reduce consequence), engineering, procedural or organisational, then GROUPED INTO OPTIONS because a regulation is adopted as a package; risk reduction re-evaluated through step 2. 4 COST BENEFIT ASSESSMENT - over the LIFE CYCLE and the whole affected fleet; costs of design, build, retrofit, training, survey, operation and lost earning capacity against benefits of fatalities and injuries averted, casualties and pollution avoided; expressed as the GROSS COST OF AVERTING A FATALITY and the NET COST, which subtracts the economic benefit the measure itself produces; used to RANK, not to decide, and NO CRITERION VALUE IS QUOTED. 5 RECOMMENDATIONS - ranked and justified, WITH THE ASSUMPTIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES EXPOSED, submitted to the Committee and independently reviewed. FSA DOES NOT DECIDE, DOES NOT MAKE A SHIP SAFE, AND CANNOT BE BETTER THAN ITS DATA.
critical_numbers: FIVE steps - and 'define the problem' is NOT one of them
Risk = frequency COMBINED WITH severity - two factors, not one
ALARP has THREE regions - intolerable, tolerable if ALARP, broadly acceptable
TWO cost-effectiveness indices - gross and net cost of averting a fatality
No mark figure is printed against this question; 16 is taken from the equal-marks rubric
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Revised Guidelines for Formal Safety Assessment for use in the IMO rule-making process, MSC-MEPC.2/Circ.12/Rev.2, issued 9 April 2018 and unrevised at this sitting - cited by identity. FSA is an IMO rule-making method and carries no Indian statutory limb.
quick_revision.major_trap: Calling 'define the problem' step 1 and pushing hazard identification to step 2. There are FIVE steps and defining the problem is preparatory work done by the decision-makers before the assessment begins. The second trap is confusing FSA with the risk assessment a Company carries out under the ISM Code: FSA studies a GENERIC model of a ship type in order to make a RULE, and it does not decide anything - it hands ranked recommendations to a Committee that does.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the five steps of FSA, and say what comes before them.
retrieval_cards.answer: Before the five, the decision-makers DEFINE THE PROBLEM - ship type, system or operation, scope, boundaries, operating conditions and existing regulations. That is preparatory and is NOT one of the steps. The five are: 1 Hazard Identification; 2 Risk Analysis; 3 Risk Control Options; 4 Cost Benefit Assessment; 5 Recommendations for decision-making.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define hazard and risk as FSA uses them.
retrieval_cards.answer: A HAZARD is a potential to threaten human life, health, property or the environment. RISK is the combination of the FREQUENCY of an occurrence and the SEVERITY of its consequence. Both factors are needed - treating risk as probability alone cannot explain why a rare catastrophe is handled differently from a frequent nuisance.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does hazard identification need both a creative and an analytical element?
retrieval_cards.answer: The creative element - a structured group review by an experienced, balanced team using what-if and hazard and operability techniques - finds hazards the data do not contain BECAUSE THEY HAVE NOT HAPPENED YET. The analytical element - casualty, incident, port State control and class defect data - makes sure the known hazards are not overlooked while the group is being imaginative. Data alone misses the novel hazard; imagination alone misses the common one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Fault tree or event tree - which runs which way, and what does each give you?
retrieval_cards.answer: A FAULT TREE runs BACKWARDS from an undesired event to the combinations of failures and conditions that could cause it, and yields FREQUENCY. An EVENT TREE runs FORWARDS from an initiating event through each barrier that may or may not succeed, and yields the spread of CONSEQUENCES and their probabilities. Joined at the accident event they form the risk contribution tree.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are GCAF and NCAF, and what is the difference between them?
retrieval_cards.answer: The GROSS cost of averting a fatality is the additional cost of a risk control option divided by the reduction in risk it achieves. The NET cost is the same calculation after SUBTRACTING the economic benefit the measure itself produces - avoided damage, avoided loss, operational saving. Where a measure pays for itself the net figure can be negative, which is the strongest case for adopting it. They RANK options; they do not decide.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between a risk control measure and a risk control option?
retrieval_cards.answer: A MEASURE is a single intervention, classified as preventive (reducing frequency) or mitigating (reducing consequence), and as engineering, procedural or organisational. An OPTION is a GROUP of measures sharing common risk-reducing attributes, assembled because a regulation is adopted as a coherent package rather than as one bolt or one procedure. The cost-benefit step evaluates options, not individual measures.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the three regions of the ALARP framework, and which one matters to step 4?
retrieval_cards.answer: An INTOLERABLE region, where risk must be reduced whatever the cost; a middle region TOLERABLE ONLY IF THE RISK IS AS LOW AS REASONABLY PRACTICABLE, where cost may properly be weighed against risk reduction; and a broadly acceptable or negligible region. The middle region is the one in which cost benefit assessment is legitimate at all.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does FSA NOT do?
retrieval_cards.answer: It does not DECIDE - it presents ranked, justified recommendations with the assumptions and uncertainties exposed, and the judgement remains with the Member States in Committee. It does not make a ship safe - it helps produce a better rule. And it cannot be better than its data: casualty data are incomplete and a generic model is an abstraction from every real ship it covers.
