blocks.h: 1. The physical basis common to all three limbs

blocks.p: Open on the physics, because all three limbs are the same physics seen in different places, and an answer that begins with paint has given away the framing.

ul: A ship's resistance divides into frictional and residuary components, and at merchant-ship speeds frictional resistance dominates. The condition of the wetted surface is therefore a fuel matter, not a cosmetic one.
Roughness thickens and disorders the turbulent boundary layer, and raises skin friction.

The penalty depends on the texture and spacing of the roughness as much as on its height. This is why a thin, even film of slime can cost more than a physical roughness of the same measured thickness - a fine, dense, disordered surface disturbs the flow far more efficiently than an occasional weld seam.

The consequence is the same in both places: more shaft power for the same speed, or speed lost at constant power. On the propeller it appears additionally as more torque for the same revolutions - the engine runs heavy, which the engineer sees in the torsionmeter, the fuel index and the exhaust temperatures long before anyone calculates a fuel penalty.

blocks.h: 2. Hull roughness - what is being managed, and the cycle that manages it

blocks.p: Begin by dividing the roughness, because the two halves behave completely differently:

ul: Physical roughness - plate waviness, weld seams, corrosion pitting, mechanical and ice damage, coating breakdown and the accumulated layers of old paint. It is largely irrecoverable and it ratchets upward over the ship's life. Each drydocking can slow the rise; none reverses it.
Biological roughness - slime, weed and hard fouling. It is recoverable, and it is where in-service effort is aimed.

blocks.p: Management is then a cycle, and giving it as a cycle is what makes this a management answer rather than a paint answer:

ul: MEASURE. Average hull roughness taken with a gauge at drydocking, over a defined pattern of readings; and in-service hull and propeller performance monitoring, comparing delivered power against speed. The monitoring is only worth anything if it is normalised for draught, trim, weather, sea state and current - otherwise the trend is noise and every conclusion drawn from it is an accident.

SPECIFY. Surface preparation standard, dry film thickness, and application quality and conditions. A poor application is itself a roughness decision - overspray, dry spray and runs create a rough surface on day one that no amount of later cleaning will recover.

CHOOSE. A coating system matched to the ship's actual trade: self-polishing copolymer, controlled depletion, or foul-release. The choice turns on service speed, activity level and idle time - foul-release systems depend on movement through the water to shed settlement, so a ship that lies idle for long periods is a poor candidate for one.

INTERVENE. Planned inspection, including the niche areas - sea chests and gratings, bow thruster tunnels, bilge keels, rudder and stern arrangements, cathodic protection anodes - which carry a disproportionate share of hard fouling and are routinely skipped. Prefer proactive grooming, which removes settlement gently and often, to reactive cleaning, which removes established fouling aggressively and late.
VERIFY. Check the result against the performance trend, not against the diver's report alone, and feed the outcome back into the next specification.

blocks.p: Two constraints belong in the answer because they bite in practice. Aggressive cleaning damages the coating and so accelerates the next fouling cycle - the cure worsening the disease. And in-water cleaning requires the permission of the port or coastal State, which is not automatic and in some places is refused, because of the release of biocides and the transfer of invasive species.

blocks.h: 3. Why it has become a duty rather than a preference

blocks.p: Hull condition used to be a matter for the owner's own economics. It is now also a regulatory and commercial obligation, and naming the driver is worth a mark.

ul: The ship energy efficiency management plan, required under the revised MARPOL Annex VI which entered into force on 1 November 2022. Hull and propeller measures are among the measures planned, implemented, monitored and evaluated within it, so the work must be documented and auditable rather than merely done.

The operational carbon intensity regime, operative from 1 January 2023 and therefore in its first year at this sitting. It makes in-service hull and propeller condition commercially visible - a fouled ship is a worse-rated ship, and charterers read the rating.

The IMO biofouling guidance, under which a ship keeps a biofouling management plan and a biofouling record book, and pays specific attention to niche areas and to in-water inspection and cleaning. This is guidance and not law, and saying so is itself a mark - though several States and ports have made parts of it a condition of entry.

The Anti-Fouling Systems Convention, under which organotin compounds acting as biocides are prohibited, and under which the control on cybutryne took effect on 1 January 2023 - six months before this sitting, and therefore operative.

blocks.h: 4. Condition-based propeller maintenance - the measurement that sets the interval

blocks.p: Define it first, because the definition is the whole limb. Condition-based propeller maintenance means the propeller is worked on when measured condition says it needs to be, and not when the calendar says so. The output of the system is a trigger, not a date.
Three independent sources of evidence feed it, and a good answer names all three:

rows: The ship says

The power-speed-revolution relationship against the baseline; heavy running - the engine making its power at lower revolutions; slip; and torsionmeter readings of shaft power and torque. All normalised for draught, trim, weather and current
The diver sees

Fouling and calcareous deposit; cavitation erosion, characteristically on the suction face near the leading edge and towards the tip; impingement attack and pitting; edge damage; and the quality of the previous polish, including coarse directional scratching left behind
The machinery tells
Stern tube bearing wear-down, stern tube oil condition and consumption, seal performance, and the blade-rate vibration signature, which changes as blade condition and wake inflow change

blocks.p: The system then works as follows:

ul: A baseline is established, ideally from sea trials or immediately after a dock polish.
The normalised trend is watched, and an agreed threshold is set - a percentage loss of performance, or an inspection grade.
Intervention is triggered when the trend or the inspection grade crosses that threshold, and is scheduled to the next convenient port with the necessary permissions.
The result is verified against the trend, which both proves the work and re-establishes the baseline.

blocks.p: The contrast with calendar-based polishing is the point of the limb. A fixed interval either sends divers to a clean propeller - money spent for nothing - or leaves a fouled propeller turning for months while the ship burns the difference. Neither is visible without measurement, which is why the calendar survives on ships that do not measure.

Its limits are real and should be stated. It requires normalised data of decent quality and a baseline to compare against; it requires a threshold that someone has actually agreed and will act on; and it requires access - port permission for in-water work, adequate water clarity, tolerable current, and conditions in which it is safe to put a diver over the side.

blocks.h: 5. Propeller coating - purpose and real limits

ul: Purpose: to resist fouling and corrosion and to hold a smooth surface for longer, so that the interval between polishes lengthens and the average roughness across the cycle falls.

Type: typically a biocide-free foul-release system - silicone or fluoropolymer - presenting a low-surface-energy, low-adhesion finish from which settlement is shed by the water flow rather than killed.

Application is the whole of it. Full cleaning, blasting and profiling of the blade, controlled temperature and humidity, and correct film thickness. A badly applied coating is worse than no coating: it raises roughness immediately and then detaches unevenly.
Benefits: slower fouling and easier subsequent cleaning, a lower average roughness across the docking cycle, and some protection against corrosion and impingement.

blocks.p: The limits are what distinguish a good answer, and they are specific:

ul: Coatings wear preferentially at the leading edge and at the tip - the highest relative velocity, and precisely the areas whose finish matters most.
Cavitation removes them locally, so a blade with an existing cavitation problem will strip its coating in exactly the region that is already suffering.

A coating is therefore a life-extender between polishes, not a substitute for polishing. A ship that coats and stops measuring has bought a longer interval and lost the ability to know when it has expired.

blocks.h: 6. Propeller polishing - method, grades, and why it pays

blocks.p: Polishing is the controlled removal of fouling, calcareous deposit and surface roughness to a specified finish. It is done in water by divers, or in dock, where a higher and more consistent standard is achievable.

ul: Cover the whole surface. Both the pressure and suction faces, and also the boss and the rope guard - the areas skipped in a hurried in-water job and the ones that quietly re-seed the blades.

Work through progressively finer grades, and never leave coarse directional scratching: a badly polished blade can be rougher than the fouled one it replaced, because the scratch pattern is regular and closely spaced, which is exactly the texture that costs most.
The leading edge and the outer radii are specified to a finer finish than the rest of the blade, because the relative velocity there is highest and they do most of the work.
Record the finish grade achieved, blade by blade, and verify against the performance trend - which closes the loop back to limb (b) and turns the polish from an event into a measurement.

blocks.p: Draw one boundary firmly, because crossing it is an operational error and not merely an examination one. Polishing does not reshape the blade. Dressing out edge damage, correcting pitch, welding and blending cavitation damage, and any removal of material that alters the section are propeller repair. They require approved procedures, a qualified repairer and class involvement, and a diver with a grinder must never be allowed to drift from one into the other.

Why it pays, in one paragraph. The propeller is a small area operating at the highest relative water velocity on the ship, and it sits at the end of the whole propulsion chain - so a few per cent lost there is a few per cent lost on everything upstream of it. Polishing is cheap, quick and can be done in water without taking the ship out of service, and its effect is felt immediately as a lighter-running engine. Of every energy-efficiency measure available to a ship in service, it has the best ratio of benefit to cost - and it is really a measurement discipline wearing the clothes of a cleaning job.

Three limbs and no printed marks, so the answer gives three roughly equal blocks. The opening physics section is what allows the three to be short: once skin friction, the boundary layer and the texture-and-spacing point are established, each limb can be written tightly without becoming thin.

Limb (a) is given two sections because it contains two different things - the maintenance cycle, and the regulatory driver that has turned it into a duty. Limb (c) is given two because the printed limb names two different activities, and a candidate who runs coating and polishing together will describe neither properly.

ul: Turning it into a paint question. The examiner asked about management, monitoring and maintenance.
Forgetting that physical roughness is irrecoverable. It is the reason a twenty-year-old hull cannot be returned to newbuild condition by cleaning.
Describing performance monitoring without normalisation. Unnormalised data is noise, and conclusions drawn from it are worse than no conclusions.
Defining condition-based maintenance as 'maintenance based on condition' and stopping. The content is the three evidence sources and the agreed threshold.
Treating a propeller coating as a permanent fix. It wears first at the leading edge and tip.
Blurring polishing into repair. Reshaping a blade is a class matter.
Drifting into a general decarbonisation essay. Name the SEEMP and the carbon intensity regime and get back to the hull.
Slime costs more than you expect. Texture and spacing matter as much as height, so a soft even film can outperform a weld seam as a source of drag.
Niche areas. Sea chests, thruster tunnels and bilge keels carry disproportionate hard fouling and are the classic omission.
Foul-release coatings are activity-dependent. They are a poor choice for a ship that lies idle.
In-water cleaning needs permission, and it is not always given.
Aggressive cleaning damages the coating and shortens the next cycle. The fix can make it worse.
A bad polish can be worse than no polish if it leaves regular coarse scratching.
The biofouling guidance is guidance, not law - though ports increasingly make parts of it a condition of entry.
Do not quote fuel-saving percentages. They are quoted freely in the trade press, vary enormously with ship and trade, and are exactly the kind of figure an examiner will ask you to justify.
Your performance monitoring shows a five per cent power increase. How do you know it is the hull and not the weather?
Why is a foul-release coating a bad idea for a ship that spends months at anchor?
Where would you expect to find cavitation erosion on a blade, and why there?
You have a diver down and he reports edge damage. What do you authorise him to do?
What is in a biofouling record book, and is it mandatory?
How does a fouled propeller show itself in the engine room?
Why polish the boss and the rope guard?

blocks.p: One physics, three views. Set up skin friction at the start and everything else hangs off it.

ul: Hull: the cycle - MEASURE, SPECIFY, CHOOSE, INTERVENE, VERIFY. And the split: physical roughness ratchets, biological roughness is recoverable.
Propeller condition: three witnesses - the ship says, the diver sees, the machinery tells - and a threshold, not a date.
Coating: buys time between polishes. Wears first where it matters most.
Polishing: restores the surface. Finer at the leading edge. Never reshape.

blocks.p: A ship pushing through water spends most of her power just rubbing against it. At the speeds merchant ships actually run, the largest single part of the resistance is skin friction - the drag of water sliding over the wetted surface - and that means the condition of that surface is not a cosmetic matter but a fuel matter. Roughen it and the thin layer of water dragged along with the hull thickens and disorders, and the drag goes up.

The counter-intuitive part is that a soft slime costs more than a hard bump of the same height. What matters is not simply how tall the roughness is but its texture and how closely spaced it is - a fine, dense, uneven surface disturbs the flow far more efficiently than an occasional weld seam. Which is why a ship that looks clean from the quay can be carrying a very expensive film.

The propeller is the same physics on a much smaller and much more sensitive area. It is turning fast, so the water goes past it faster than past anything else on the ship, and a little roughness there costs disproportionately. A rough propeller also makes the engine work harder for the same speed - it runs heavy - which the engineer feels as higher torque and higher exhaust temperatures long before anyone calculates a fuel penalty.

So the whole of this question is one idea seen three ways: keep the surfaces smooth, and know when they have stopped being smooth. The second half is the harder one. You cannot see the hull, and the ship's own performance is buried under weather, loading and current - so the real skill is not the cleaning but the measurement that tells you when cleaning is worth doing. That is why the middle limb is about condition rather than about a calendar.

steps.title: The physical basis common to all three limbs
points: Resistance divides into FRICTIONAL and RESIDUARY, and friction dominates at merchant-ship speeds - so surface condition is a fuel matter

Roughness thickens and disorders the turbulent boundary layer and raises skin friction; the penalty depends on TEXTURE AND SPACING as well as height, which is why slime costs more than physical roughness of the same thickness
Consequence: more shaft power for the same speed, or speed lost at constant power - and on the propeller more torque, so the ENGINE RUNS HEAVY

steps.title: Hull roughness - what is being managed, and the cycle that manages it
points: TWO COMPONENTS: PHYSICAL roughness - plate waviness, weld seams, pitting, mechanical damage, coating breakdown and accumulated layers - which is largely IRRECOVERABLE and RATCHETS UPWARD; and BIOLOGICAL roughness - slime, weed and hard fouling - which is recoverable
MEASURE: average hull roughness taken at dock, and in-service performance monitoring NORMALISED for draught, trim, weather and current, without which the trend is noise

SPECIFY, CHOOSE, INTERVENE, VERIFY: surface preparation, film thickness and application quality; a coating system matched to speed, idle time and trade; inspection INCLUDING NICHE AREAS, with grooming preferred to reactive cleaning; and verification against the performance trend. Two constraints - aggressive cleaning damages the coating, and in-water cleaning needs permission that is not automatic

steps.title: Why it has become a duty rather than a preference
points: The SEEMP under the revised MARPOL Annex VI, in force 1 November 2022 - hull and propeller measures are planned, implemented, monitored and evaluated, so the work is documented and auditable
The OPERATIONAL CARBON INTENSITY regime, operative from 1 January 2023, which makes in-service condition commercially visible to charterers as well as to the flag State

The IMO biofouling guidance - a biofouling management plan and record book, niche areas, in-water inspection and cleaning - GUIDANCE, NOT LAW; and the Anti-Fouling Convention, organotin prohibited, with the cybutryne control effective 1 January 2023 and therefore operative at this sitting

steps.title: Condition-based propeller maintenance - the measurement that sets the interval
points: DEFINITION: the propeller is worked on when MEASURED CONDITION says so, not when the calendar says so. The output is a TRIGGER, not a date

THREE SOURCES OF EVIDENCE. THE SHIP SAYS: the power-speed-revolution relationship, heavy running, slip and torsionmeter readings, all normalised. THE DIVER SEES: fouling and calcareous deposit, cavitation erosion on the suction face near the leading edge and tip, impingement and pitting, edge damage, poor previous polish. THE MACHINERY TELLS: bearing wear-down, stern tube oil condition, seal performance and blade-rate vibration

Intervention when the trend or the inspection grade crosses an AGREED THRESHOLD. Contrast with calendar polishing, which either wastes money or leaves a fouled propeller turning. LIMITS: it needs normalised data, a baseline, an agreed threshold, and access - permission, water clarity, current and diver safety

steps.title: Propeller coating - purpose and real limits
points: PURPOSE: resist fouling and corrosion and hold a smooth surface for longer, LENGTHENING THE POLISH INTERVAL

Typically a biocide-free foul-release silicone or fluoropolymer presenting a low-adhesion surface; application demands full cleaning, blasting and profiling, controlled conditions and correct film thickness - A BAD APPLICATION IS WORSE THAN NONE

LIMITS, and they are the mark: coatings wear preferentially at the LEADING EDGE AND TIP, exactly where it matters most, and cavitation removes them locally. A coating is a LIFE-EXTENDER BETWEEN POLISHES, NOT A SUBSTITUTE FOR POLISHING

steps.title: Propeller polishing - method, grades, and why it pays
points: Controlled removal of fouling, calcareous deposit and roughness to a specified finish - in water by divers, or in dock to a higher standard. Both faces, plus the boss and rope guard, which are the areas skipped in a hurried job

Work through progressively finer grades, never leaving coarse directional scratching; the LEADING EDGE AND OUTER RADII are specified finer because they do the work. RECORD THE GRADE and verify against the performance trend, closing the loop from limb (b)

DO NOT RESHAPE. Dressing edge damage, pitch correction and cavitation repair are propeller REPAIR, requiring approved procedures and class involvement. WHY IT PAYS: a small area at high relative velocity sets the efficiency of the whole chain; it is cheap, quick, done in water, and it unloads the engine

questions.memory_cue: One physics, three views: SKIN FRICTION at (1); the hull CYCLE - measure, specify, choose, intervene, verify - at (2); the DUTY at (3); the propeller TRIGGER at (4); COATING buys time (5) and POLISHING restores the surface (6).

quick_revision.major_trap: Answering it as a paint question. The examiner asked about MANAGEMENT, MONITORING and MAINTENANCE, and the three limbs are a cycle: measure the condition, decide from the measurement, restore the surface, verify against the trend. The second trap is blurring POLISHING into REPAIR - dressing edge damage, correcting pitch or blending cavitation damage alters the blade section, is propeller repair, and requires approved procedures and class involvement. The third is forgetting that PHYSICAL hull roughness is largely irrecoverable and ratchets upward, which is why no amount of cleaning returns an old hull to newbuild condition.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the two components of hull roughness, and how do they differ?
retrieval_cards.answer: PHYSICAL roughness - plate waviness, weld seams, corrosion pitting, mechanical damage, coating breakdown and accumulated layers of old paint - is LARGELY IRRECOVERABLE and ratchets upward over the ship's life; each docking can slow the rise, none reverses it. BIOLOGICAL roughness - slime, weed and hard fouling - is RECOVERABLE, and is where in-service effort is aimed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why can a thin film of slime cost more than a physical roughness of the same height?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the drag penalty depends on the TEXTURE AND SPACING of the roughness as well as on its height. A fine, dense, disordered surface disturbs the turbulent boundary layer far more efficiently than an occasional weld seam of the same measured thickness. It is also why a badly polished propeller, left with regular coarse scratching, can be rougher in effect than the fouled blade it replaced.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the hull roughness management cycle in order.
retrieval_cards.answer: MEASURE - average hull roughness at dock, and in-service performance monitoring normalised for draught, trim, weather and current. SPECIFY - surface preparation, film thickness and application quality. CHOOSE - a coating system matched to speed, activity and idle time. INTERVENE - inspection including niche areas, with grooming preferred to reactive cleaning. VERIFY - against the performance trend, feeding back into the next specification.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What makes propeller maintenance 'condition based', and what are the three sources of evidence?
retrieval_cards.answer: The propeller is worked on when measured condition crosses an agreed threshold, not when the calendar says so - the output is a TRIGGER, not a date. THE SHIP SAYS: the normalised power-speed-revolution relationship, heavy running, slip and torsionmeter readings. THE DIVER SEES: fouling and calcareous deposit, cavitation erosion near the leading edge and tip, impingement, edge damage and poor previous polish. THE MACHINERY TELLS: stern tube bearing wear-down, oil condition, seal performance and blade-rate vibration.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does a propeller coating fail first, and what follows from that?
retrieval_cards.answer: At the LEADING EDGE and the TIP - the highest relative velocity, and exactly the areas whose finish matters most - and locally wherever cavitation is occurring. It follows that a coating is a LIFE-EXTENDER BETWEEN POLISHES and not a substitute for polishing, and that a ship which coats and then stops measuring has bought a longer interval and lost the ability to know when it has expired.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is a propeller polished properly, and what must a diver NOT do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Remove fouling, calcareous deposit and roughness from both faces and from the boss and rope guard, working through progressively finer grades and never leaving coarse directional scratching; the leading edge and outer radii are specified to a finer finish because they do most of the work. Record the grade achieved and verify against the performance trend. HE MUST NOT RESHAPE THE BLADE - dressing edge damage, correcting pitch and blending cavitation damage are propeller REPAIR, requiring approved procedures and class involvement.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What makes hull and propeller condition a regulatory duty rather than an owner's choice?
retrieval_cards.answer: The ship energy efficiency management plan required under the revised MARPOL Annex VI, in force 1 November 2022, within which hull and propeller measures are planned, implemented, monitored and evaluated - so the work must be documented and auditable. And the operational carbon intensity regime, operative from 1 January 2023, which makes in-service condition commercially visible to charterers as well as to the flag State. The IMO biofouling guidance sits alongside as GUIDANCE, not law.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name two practical constraints on in-water hull cleaning.
retrieval_cards.answer: Aggressive cleaning DAMAGES THE COATING and so accelerates the next fouling cycle - the cure worsening the disease, which is why proactive grooming is preferred to reactive cleaning. And in-water cleaning requires the PERMISSION of the port or coastal State, which is not automatic and is refused in some places, because of biocide release and the transfer of invasive species.

blocks.h: 1. What has actually happened - three events in one casualty

blocks.p: Read the printed facts before reaching for the statute, because they decide which powers are engaged. This casualty contains three events:

ul: A collision - engaging the duties of both masters, and in due course the apportionment of fault between the vessels;
Loss of life - which makes this a very serious marine casualty, and that classification is what makes the safety investigation mandatory rather than discretionary;
Damage to the vessels - raising seaworthiness, survey, class, detention and possibly salvage.

blocks.p: And one event that has NOT occurred: there is no oil spill. The stem says only that lives were lost and the vessel damaged. That absence is load-bearing. The stem nevertheless still asks about the marine environment, so the environmental limb survives - but it survives as a duty to prevent a discharge from a damaged ship that threatens one, not as a response to pollution that has happened. An answer describing booms, skimmers and shoreline clean-up has answered a different casualty.

The governing statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, and it is worth noticing what kind of statute it is: as much a grant of powers as a list of prohibitions. Almost every step below is somebody exercising a power the Act confers - to detain, to direct, to inquire, to act and recover the cost.

blocks.h: 2. Immediate steps on board - the Master, and the order matters

blocks.p: The master initiates all of this, because he is the only person present. The order is itself examinable.

ul: Muster, account for all persons on board, and search for the missing. Lives come before the ship. This is the overriding first duty and it precedes damage assessment and reporting.

Render assistance to the other vessel, her master, crew and passengers, so far as he can do so without serious danger to his own ship and those on board; stand by; and exchange the identifying particulars of his own ship - her name, port of registry and the ports she is coming from and going to. Failure to comply with this duty is an offence, and it also raises a presumption that the collision was caused by his wrongful act, neglect or default.

Assess the ship. Sound all tanks, bilges and compartments; establish the extent and location of the damage; contain flooding and close watertight boundaries; and assess stability and residual longitudinal strength before moving the ship at all - a damaged ship put on a course or a speed she can no longer take is how a survivable casualty becomes a total loss.

Prevent a discharge. Isolate the threatened tank, transfer oil internally to sound tanks where it is safe to do so, and implement the shipboard oil pollution emergency plan against the probability of a release rather than against one that has happened.
Broadcast and report. A distress or urgency message as the situation requires; and a danger message where the casualty endangers navigation.

Preserve the evidence. Secure the voyage data recorder before it overwrites; preserve charts, the bridge and engine room log books, the movement book, course and engine order recorders, alarm and event printouts, and note the position and time. This is a first-hour duty, not an afterthought, and on the engineering side it is the Chief Engineer's.

blocks.h: 4. Steps for the safety of the ships

blocks.p: Both ships, not only the Indian-flag one.

ul: Damage survey by the classification society and by the Administration's surveyor. Repairs, or an approved temporary repair, before the ship proceeds, with conditions of class imposed and a voyage plan agreed where she is permitted to move to a repair port.

Detention. Where a ship is unsafe by reason of damage, defective equipment, undermanning or overloading, the Director-General or an authorised surveyor may provisionally detain her. This is the power that converts an opinion about seaworthiness into an enforceable prohibition on sailing.
Salvage and towage where the ship cannot proceed under her own power - commonly engaged on Lloyd's Open Form, under the salvage provisions of the Act and the rules made under it.

A place of refuge. Where a damaged ship needs sheltered water, the decision is the coastal State's alone and there is no right to one. It is made under the IMO Assembly guidelines on places of refuge then operative, read with the resolution on maritime assistance services, balancing the risk to the ship against the risk to the coast.

Directions. The Act empowers the Central Government to give directions to the owner, the master or the salvor as to what shall or shall not be done. This is the power that makes a course of action compellable rather than merely recommended, and it is the answer to 'who should initiate' when the owner will not.
Navigational safety - marking the casualty, navigational warnings to shipping, and an exclusion zone around the site where necessary.

blocks.h: 5. Steps for the marine environment - preventive, because nothing has yet escaped

blocks.p: The whole of this section is contingent, and saying so is what makes it correct on these facts.

ul: The ship acts first. The shipboard oil pollution emergency plan is implemented; the threatened tank is isolated; oil is transferred internally where it is safe; leaks are plugged and patched; and the ship rigs her own containment as far as she is able.

The risk is assessed and declared honestly - the quantity and grade of oil in the threatened spaces, the condition of the boundaries retaining it, and the realistic worst case. Understating it to avoid a detention is the single worst decision available at this point.

The Indian Coast Guard and the national oil spill contingency plan are placed on READINESS, not on response. Equipment and personnel are mobilised to a state of preparedness; nothing is deployed against a spill that has not occurred.

The legal engine is the Part of the Act empowering the Central Government, where a casualty creates a risk of pollution, to give directions, to take such action itself as it considers necessary, and to recover the cost of doing so. The power reaches a THREATENED escape and not only an actual one - which is precisely why it applies on facts where nothing has yet been spilt.
Co-ordination with the State pollution control board, the fisheries and environment authorities and the port authority.

Funding is already in place - through the P&I club and, where the ship carries the appropriate certificate, through the compulsory pollution insurance with a right of direct action against the insurer.

blocks.h: 6. Investigation and inquiry - two systems, and both are engaged

blocks.p: There are two, they run in parallel, and confusing them is the classic error.
The national system, under the Act:

ul: the report of the casualty by the master or owner;
a preliminary inquiry by a person appointed for the purpose - a surveyor or other officer - to establish what happened and whether more is needed;
a formal investigation before a court with assessors, which may find fault and which may cancel or suspend the certificate of a master, mate or engineer. It is therefore partly disciplinary.

blocks.p: The international system:

ul: the Casualty Investigation Code, made mandatory through SOLAS chapter XI-1;

mandatory here, because a death makes this a very serious marine casualty. Note that the environmental trigger for the same obligation requires severe damage to the environment, and there has been none - so it is the loss of life alone that compels the investigation;
India, as flag State, is the marine safety investigating State; the other vessel's flag State, if foreign, is a substantially interested State and may participate; and the report is submitted to IMO.
Its purpose is the prevention of recurrence, and it is expressly NOT the apportionment of blame or the determination of liability.

blocks.p: Hold the two apart in the answer. One can take a man's certificate away; the other must not apportion blame at all. A candidate who merges them has misdescribed both.

blocks.h: 7. Liability, and a direct answer to the examiner's 'who'

ul: Collision liability is apportioned by degree of fault, on the COLREG breaches established by the evidence. The doctrine of apportionment is the subject of a separate question on this paper and is not repeated here.

Claims lie in the admiralty jurisdiction of the High Courts under the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 - in rem against the ship, with arrest and the provision of security, or in personam against the owner.
Claims for loss of life and personal injury carry a maritime lien, ranking second in the priority of liens, after crew wages.

Limitation. The owner may limit his liability by tonnage under the limitation convention as amended, unless the loss resulted from his personal act or omission committed with intent or recklessly and with knowledge.
Pollution liability arises only if a discharge follows, and is stated conditionally for that reason: strict, channelled to the registered owner, and backed by compulsory insurance.

blocks.p: The examiner asked who should initiate. Answer it directly:

rows: The Master
Muster and search; assistance and standing by; damage and stability assessment; discharge prevention; broadcasts; evidence preservation; and every first report
The owner and the Designated Person
The company emergency response, the surveys, salvage engagement, insurers and class
The Director-General / DG Shipping
Detention of an unsafe ship; directions; the preliminary inquiry and the formal investigation; and notification of the other flag State
The Central Government
Directions and intervention where pollution is threatened, and recovery of the cost
The Indian Coast Guard
Search and rescue; pollution readiness and, if needed, response at sea
The coastal State - and nobody else
The decision whether to grant a place of refuge

blocks.p: The question asks two things - what steps and who initiates them - and an answer that gives only the first loses half of it. The 'who' is therefore answered inside every section and again in a table at the close, which costs four lines and directly answers the printed words.

Section 1 is the section that makes the rest correct. Identifying the three events, and expressly identifying the fourth that has not happened, is what stops the answer sliding into a spill-response essay - and it takes six lines.

ul: Inventing an oil spill. The stem says lives lost and vessel damaged. Nothing has escaped. The environmental duty here is preventive.
Giving the master's duties out of order. Muster and search for the missing come first.
Merging the two investigations. The national formal investigation may cancel a certificate; the international safety investigation must not apportion blame.
Saying a damaged ship has a right to a place of refuge. She does not. The coastal State decides.
Forgetting the other ship. The question says 'the ships', plural.
Omitting evidence preservation, and in particular the VDR, which overwrites.
Answering 'who' with a single authority. The statute distributes the initiative deliberately.
Loss of life is what makes the safety investigation mandatory. The environmental trigger requires SEVERE damage to the environment, which has not occurred - so do not reach for it.
The MARPOL Protocol I report is triggered by a PROBABILITY of discharge. No actual escape is needed, which is exactly the point on these facts.
The statutory environmental power reaches prevention, not only containment. A candidate who thinks the power only bites after a spill will conclude, wrongly, that there is nothing to say.
Failure to stand by is both an offence and the trigger for a presumption of fault. Two consequences, not one.
Detention is provisional and is exercised by the Director-General or an authorised surveyor - not by the port, not by class, and not by the coast guard.
Loss of life claims rank SECOND among maritime liens, after crew wages.
The administration at this sitting is DG Shipping. The later renaming belongs to a statute that is years away from this paper.
Assess stability and residual strength BEFORE moving. The instinct to make for port is how damaged ships are lost.
Nothing has been spilt. Why are you reporting anything to the coastal State at all?
Your ship is holed and you are two hours from a sheltered bay. Can you go in?
What is the difference between the preliminary inquiry and the formal investigation?
Who can stop your ship from sailing, and on what grounds?
As Chief Engineer, what do you do in the first thirty minutes?
The other ship is foreign-flagged. What difference does that make to the investigation?
Why must the safety investigation not apportion blame?

blocks.p: Three events, four actions, two inquiries.

ul: Three events - collision, loss of life, damage. And the fourth that did not happen: no spill.

Four actions - on board (muster, assist, assess, prevent, preserve), tell (owner, DG Shipping, Coast Guard, coastal State, insurers, other flag), the ships (survey, detain, salvage, refuge, directions), the environment (SOPEP, declare, readiness, directions and intervention).
Two inquiries - the national one that can take a certificate; the international one that must not apportion blame.

blocks.p: Then one line for the 'who': master initiates, owner responds, Director-General detains and inquires, Coast Guard executes, coastal State decides on refuge.

blocks.p: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is not held by the True Source corpus at 319524c, and this is the sharpest example of the register inversion on the paper. The corpus's India holdings are the Admiralty Act 2017, the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 and the Coastal Shipping Act 2025 - and two of those three are future at this sitting. The instrument physically present in the corpus is the prohibited one. Nothing from the 2025 Act is consumed, and no 2025 section number appears anywhere.

The 1958 Act's provisions are therefore authoritative secondary, carried through an MIW answer to the character-identical stem authored under the same statute three months earlier and integrated on the main line. That is a strong form of secondary evidence - the same question, the same year, the same Act - but it is secondary, and it is recorded as such.
The Admiralty Act, 2017 is held and was read verbatim, so the maritime lien priority placing loss of life second, after crew wages, carries primary support.

The administration at this sitting is DG Shipping. The renaming followed the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 and took effect in 2026, roughly thirty-two months after this paper. It appears nowhere in this answer as the operative body.

The places-of-refuge guidance is stated without a resolution number. The instrument operative at this sitting was superseded by a 33rd Assembly resolution adopted on 6 December 2023 - five months after this sitting - and the corpus register, being maintained for the present, marks the operative one as stale and the future one as current. That is the inversion in miniature. The framework is described; the number is not asserted.

blocks.p: Two ships have hit each other near the Indian coast. People are dead, both ships are damaged, and the question is a practical one: what now, and who starts it?

The useful way to hold this is that one accident has produced three separate problems, each with its own machinery. There is a collision, which raises duties on both masters and a later argument about whose fault it was. There is loss of life, which is what turns this from a bad day into the most serious category of casualty the system recognises - and that category makes an official investigation compulsory rather than optional. And there is damage to the ships, which raises whether either is fit to move at all.

What the stem does not say is as important as what it does. Nothing has been spilt. So the environmental half of the question is not about cleaning up - it is about a damaged ship that might spill, and about the powers that exist to make somebody act before she does. That is a real distinction: the statute's environmental powers are drafted to reach a threatened escape and not only an actual one, which is exactly why they still apply here.

And notice what kind of statute this is. It is not mainly a list of things you must not do. It is a grant of powers - to detain a ship, to direct her, to inquire into what happened, to take action yourself and send the bill. So the answer to the examiner's 'who' is never one person. The master starts almost everything, because he is the only one there; the owner and the company respond; the administration detains, directs and investigates; the coast guard executes at sea; and the coastal State - nobody else - decides whether a damaged ship may come in. Getting those roles the right way round is most of the marks.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A procedural question with two named objectives - the safety of the ships, and the marine environment - and an express demand for the ACTOR at each step ('who should initiate such steps'). The examiner is testing whether the candidate can sequence a casualty response under a statute rather than list statutory powers. The load-bearing reading is that the printed facts contain THREE events and not four: collision, loss of life, damage - and NO oil spill. That absence converts the environmental limb from a response question into a PREVENTION question, and an answer that describes booms, skimmers and shoreline clean-up has answered a casualty this examiner did not set.

Recorded at 16 on the equal-marks rubric. Planned as: a short framing section identifying the three events; then immediate action, reporting, safety of the ships and the environment as the four substantive blocks; then investigation and liability. The 'who' is answered inside every block and again explicitly at the close, because it is half of what was asked.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That loss of life is recognised as making this a VERY SERIOUS MARINE CASUALTY, which is what makes the safety investigation mandatory. That the master's immediate duties are given IN ORDER, with muster and search for the missing before anything else. That the statutory powers are named - detention, directions, inquiry - with the correct actor against each. quick_revision.major_trap: Inventing an oil spill. The stem prints only that lives were lost and the vessel damaged, so the casualty contains THREE events and not four, and the environmental limb is a duty to PREVENT a discharge rather than a response to one. The statutory power still applies, because it reaches a THREATENED escape as well as an actual one - but booms, skimmers, dispersant and shoreline clean-up describe a casualty this examiner did not set. The second trap is merging the two investigations: the national formal investigation may cancel or suspend a certificate, while the international safety investigation exists to prevent recurrence and must not apportion blame.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How many events does this casualty contain, and which one has NOT happened?
retrieval_cards.answer: THREE - a collision, loss of life, and damage to the vessels. There is NO oil spill; the stem says only that lives were lost and the vessel damaged. The environmental limb therefore survives as a duty to PREVENT a discharge from a ship that threatens one, not as a response to pollution that has occurred, and the statutory intervention power applies because it reaches a threatened escape as well as an actual one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the master's immediate duties in order.
retrieval_cards.answer: Muster, account for all persons and search for the missing. Render assistance to the other vessel and those on board so far as he can without serious danger to his own ship; stand by; exchange his ship's identifying particulars. Sound tanks, assess damage, contain flooding and assess stability and residual strength BEFORE MOVING. Prevent a discharge - isolate, transfer internally, implement the SOPEP. Broadcast distress or urgency and a danger message. Preserve the evidence, VDR first, before it overwrites.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the two investigations, and what may each do?
retrieval_cards.answer: NATIONAL, under the Act: a report, a preliminary inquiry by an appointed person, then a formal investigation before a court with assessors, which may find fault and MAY CANCEL OR SUSPEND a certificate - it is partly disciplinary. INTERNATIONAL: the Casualty Investigation Code, mandatory through SOLAS chapter XI-1, whose purpose is the PREVENTION OF RECURRENCE and which is expressly NOT to apportion blame or determine liability.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What makes the safety investigation mandatory on these facts?
retrieval_cards.answer: The LOSS OF LIFE, which makes this a VERY SERIOUS MARINE CASUALTY. Note that the alternative environmental trigger for the same obligation requires SEVERE damage to the environment, and there has been none - so it is the death alone that compels the investigation. India as flag State is the marine safety investigating State; a foreign second flag is a substantially interested State.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does a damaged ship have a right to a place of refuge?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The decision belongs to the coastal State alone, made under the IMO Assembly guidelines on places of refuge read with the maritime assistance services resolution, balancing the risk to the ship against the risk to the coast. There is no right, and a master who assumes one may find himself ordered to remain offshore.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Nothing has been spilt. What environmental steps are nevertheless required, and by whom?
retrieval_cards.answer: The ship acts first - SOPEP, isolate the threatened tank, transfer internally, plug and patch, rig her own containment - and the master assesses and declares the risk honestly. The Coast Guard and the national contingency plan are placed on READINESS, not response. The Central Government may give DIRECTIONS, may take action itself, and may RECOVER THE COST; the power reaches a threatened escape and not only an actual one. And a MARPOL Protocol I report is due, because a PROBABILITY of discharge is enough to trigger it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where do claims for loss of life rank among maritime liens, and where are they brought?
retrieval_cards.answer: SECOND, after crew wages. They are brought in the admiralty jurisdiction of the High Courts under the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 - in rem against the ship, with arrest and the provision of security, or in personam against the owner.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The examiner asks WHO should initiate. Answer it.
retrieval_cards.answer: The MASTER initiates almost everything, because he is the only one present - muster, assistance, assessment, prevention, broadcasts, evidence and every first report. The OWNER AND DESIGNATED PERSON respond and engage surveyors, salvors, class and insurers. The DIRECTOR-GENERAL detains, directs, and holds the preliminary inquiry and formal investigation. The CENTRAL GOVERNMENT directs and intervenes where pollution is threatened, and recovers the cost. The COAST GUARD executes at sea. The COASTAL STATE, and nobody else, decides on a place of refuge.

blocks.h: 1. What the Act means by an unseaworthy ship

blocks.p: Begin with an honest statement about the Act's structure, because it is itself a mark. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 carries no separate definitions entry for 'unseaworthy'. The meaning is drawn from the section that creates the offence of sending an unseaworthy ship to sea, which describes the condition by listing what fitness is measured against.
A ship is unseaworthy where, by reason of any of the following, she is not fit to proceed to sea:

ul: the materials of which she is made, and her construction;
the qualifications of the master;
the number, description and qualifications of the crew, including the officers;
the weight, description and stowage of the cargo and ballast;
the condition of her hull and equipment, and of her boilers and machinery.

blocks.p: And the closing formula is the test itself: she must be fit in every respect to proceed on the proposed voyage or service without serious danger to human life.
Two features of that test are what the examiner is looking for.

ul: It reaches far beyond steel. The crew and the stowage are in the list. A structurally perfect ship with a full set of certificates can be unseaworthy because she is undermanned, or because her officers hold the wrong certificates for the trade, or because her cargo has been stowed so as to make her unstable or overstressed. Candidates who describe only hull and machinery have given a third of the definition.

It is relative, not absolute. Fitness is judged against the proposed voyage or service. The same ship may be entirely fit for a short coastal passage in fine weather and unfit for a winter ocean crossing, without anything about her having changed. Seaworthiness is a relationship between a ship and a job, and saying so is what turns a list into an answer.

blocks.h: 2. The offence, and the defences the Act allows

blocks.p: The definition exists because the Act builds an offence on it:

ul: it is an offence for a person to send or attempt to send an Indian ship to sea in an unseaworthy state;
and it is a separate offence for a master who knowingly takes her to sea in that state.
The threshold in both cases is that the life of any person is likely to be thereby endangered. Not every unfitness is criminal - the unfitness must endanger life.

blocks.p: The Act allows two defences, and knowing them is what distinguishes a precise answer:

ul: that he used all reasonable means to ensure her being sent to sea in a seaworthy state; or
that sending or taking her to sea in that state was, under the circumstances, reasonable and justifiable - and the Act places the burden of proving that on him.

blocks.p: There is also a procedural protection: no prosecution is instituted except by, or with the consent of, the Central Government. That is not a technicality. It exists because a criminal charge against an owner or master over a matter of seaworthiness is a serious step, and the Act reserves the decision to take it.

blocks.h: 3. What an unsafe ship is, and the power to detain her

blocks.p: 'Unsafe' is a different provision doing a different job. A ship is unsafe where, by reason of:

ul: the defective condition of her hull, equipment or machinery; or
overloading or improper loading,

blocks.p: she is unfit to proceed to sea without serious danger to human life, having regard to the nature of the service for which she is intended. Note that the same relative test appears - fitness is measured against the intended service, not in the abstract.
The consequence is a power, and its shape matters:

ul: the ship may be provisionally detained for the purpose of survey;
a written statement of the grounds is served on the master forthwith, so that the owner knows the case he has to meet;
a survey follows, by a surveyor or a competent person appointed for the purpose;
on the report, the ship is either released or finally detained until the defects are made good to the satisfaction of the Administration;

and there is provision for compensation where a ship has been detained without sufficient reason - the discipline on the power, and the counterpart of the fact that it can be exercised on an opinion rather than on proof.

blocks.h: 4. The real difference between the two

blocks.p: The examiner has asked for the difference. Give it as a difference in kind, because that is what it is.

blocks.p: The relationship between them, stated as a rule: every unsafe ship is unseaworthy, but not every unseaworthy ship is unsafe within the meaning of the detention power. A ship that is structurally sound and correctly loaded but seriously undermanned, or whose chief engineer holds no valid certificate for her, is unseaworthy - yet she does not fall within the listed causes of the detention provision. In practice the gap is closed by other machinery: the safe manning document, the certificates themselves, and port State control.

blocks.h: 5. The owner's obligation to the crew

blocks.p: This is the most quietly forceful provision in the area, and its force is in how it operates rather than in what it requires.

ul: It is IMPLIED. The obligation is implied into every contract of service between the owner and the master or a seaman, and into every contract of apprenticeship to the sea service. Nobody has to write it in, and its absence from the agreement means nothing.

It operates NOTWITHSTANDING ANY AGREEMENT TO THE CONTRARY. It cannot be excluded, limited or waived - not by the contract, and not by the seafarer himself. This is the heart of it: the person the obligation protects is the person with least power to refuse to sail, so the law removes his capacity to give the protection away.

It binds more than the owner. The obligation lies on the owner, on the master, and on every agent charged with the loading of the ship or the preparing of her for sea or the sending of her to sea - so responsibility follows the function and cannot be arranged out of existence by interposing a manager or an agent.

Its content is twofold. To use all reasonable means to ensure the seaworthiness of the ship for the voyage at the time when the voyage commences; and to keep her in a seaworthy condition during the voyage.

blocks.p: The second half of that is the part candidates omit, and it is the operationally important one. The duty does not discharge itself at the moment of departure. It is a continuing obligation throughout the voyage - which is precisely why a defect arising at sea, ignored, is a breach, and why the planned maintenance system, the defect list and the reporting of defects to the company are the machinery by which an owner actually performs it.

Note also what the standard is: all reasonable means, not a guarantee. The Act does not make the owner an insurer of the ship's condition; it requires him to have done everything reasonable. That is the same standard as the first defence to the offence, and the two provisions read together.

blocks.h: 6. How the obligation is policed, and the statute in force at this sitting

ul: Under the Act itself, the Central Government may cause a ship to be surveyed where a complaint is made that she is unseaworthy, and the detention machinery in section 3 above stands behind it.

In practice the obligation is policed by the classification society at periodical and occasional survey, by flag State survey and certification, by ISM internal and external audit of the safety management system, and by port State control in every port the ship enters.

And by the seafarer himself - through the on-board complaint procedure, through complaint to the flag State administration, and through complaint to an authorized officer in a port of call. The statutory obligation and the labour-convention machinery reinforce one another: the Act says the ship must be kept seaworthy, and the complaint machinery is how the man on board says that she is not.

blocks.p: Close on the statute, because the question says 'as amended' and invites the point. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is the operative statute at this sitting, and there is nothing else in the field. The Act that eventually replaced it did not exist in any form at this date - not as an Act, and not as a Bill before either House. Every proposition above is given on the 1958 Act as it then stood.

Three questions are asked in one paragraph and the answer gives them three blocks, with the first taking two sections because the definition and the offence built on it are separate things. No mark figure is printed, so the blocks are roughly equal - and deliberately not weighted 5/6/5, notwithstanding that another sitting of the same three questions prints exactly that split across lettered limbs.

The table at section 4 is where the marks are. The examiner asked for a difference, and a table that distinguishes the two on five axes answers that word directly, in less space than prose would take.

The Act has no definitions entry for 'unseaworthy'. Saying so is more impressive than inventing one.

blocks.p: One phrase carries the definition: fit in every respect to proceed on the proposed voyage or service. Hang the five heads off it - materials and construction, master, crew, cargo and ballast, hull and machinery - and note that two of the five are about people and cargo rather than about the ship.
Then two words and two mechanisms:

ul: UNSEAWORTHY = STATE + OFFENCE. Wide, retrospective, needs a prosecution.
UNSAFE = LISTED CAUSE + POWER. Narrow, preventive, needs an opinion and a survey.
The overlap runs one way: every unsafe ship is unseaworthy; not the converse.

blocks.p: And for the last part, one sentence: implied into every contract, cannot be signed away, binds the agent too, and continues throughout the voyage.

The corpus's India holdings are the Admiralty Act 2017, the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 and the Coastal Shipping Act 2025 - and two of those three are future at this sitting. The temporal position on this question is unusually simple, and simpler than at any later sitting of the same stem. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 was the operative law throughout, and at July 2023 its replacement did not exist in any form: the Bill was not introduced in the Lok Sabha until December 2024, seventeen months after this paper, and the Act that repealed the 1958 Act commenced only in March 2026. blocks.p: Everyone knows roughly what an unseaworthy ship is - one that is not fit to go. The point of this question is that the statute means something wider and more practical than the picture the phrase conjures. Fitness is not only about steel. A ship in perfect structural condition, with a full set of certificates, can be unfit to sail because she has too few people on board, or the wrong people, or because her cargo has been stowed in a way that will make her behave badly at sea.

So the test the law applies is deliberately open: is she fit, in every respect, for the particular voyage she is about to make, with the particular people and the particular cargo she has? The same ship can be perfectly fit for a short coastal run and unfit for a winter ocean passage, and nothing about her has changed. Fitness is measured against the job, not in the abstract.

The second half of the question turns on a distinction that looks like word-play and is not. One of the two terms describes a condition the ship is in, and the law's response to it is to punish somebody afterwards for having sent her to sea in it. The other is the trigger for a power - it lets an official stop the ship at the quay, now, before anything happens. The first is retrospective and needs a prosecution; the second is preventive and needs only an opinion honestly formed. That is why the second is drafted more narrowly and lists the things that can cause it: a power to stop a ship sailing has to be exercisable quickly and on visible grounds.

The last part is about the crew, and it contains the most quietly forceful provision in the whole area. The duty to keep the ship fit is written into every seafarer's contract whether or not anybody put it there - and it cannot be signed away. A crew member who agreed to sail on an unfit ship would still have the benefit of it. That matters because the person with least power to refuse is the one the obligation protects.

quick_revision.major_trap: Treating 'unseaworthy' and 'unsafe' as the same idea in different words. They differ in KIND: unseaworthiness is a STATE, defined widely enough to include the crew and the stowage, and the law's response is an OFFENCE punished after the fact; an unsafe ship is a TRIGGER FOR A POWER, defined narrowly by listed causes, and the response is DETENTION before the fact. The overlap runs one way only - every unsafe ship is unseaworthy, but a sound ship that is seriously undermanned is unseaworthy without falling within the detention provision. The second trap is stopping the owner's obligation at departure: it is implied, unwaivable, binds the loading agent too, and CONTINUES THROUGHOUT THE VOYAGE.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 mean by an unseaworthy ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Act has no separate definitions entry; the meaning comes from the section creating the offence. A ship is unseaworthy where, by reason of the materials of which she is made and her construction, the qualifications of the master, the number, description and qualifications of the crew, the weight, description and stowage of cargo and ballast, or the condition of her hull, equipment, boilers and machinery, she is not FIT IN EVERY RESPECT TO PROCEED ON THE PROPOSED VOYAGE OR SERVICE without serious danger to human life.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Can a structurally perfect, fully certificated ship be unseaworthy?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes. The crew and the cargo are in the statutory list. A ship in perfect structural condition can be unseaworthy because she is undermanned, because her officers hold the wrong certificates for the service, or because her cargo has been stowed so as to make her unstable or overstressed. Fitness is also RELATIVE to the proposed voyage, so the same ship may be fit for a coastal run and unfit for an ocean passage without anything about her having changed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does an unsafe ship differ from an unseaworthy ship, and which way does the overlap run?
retrieval_cards.answer: Unseaworthy is a STATE and the law's response is an OFFENCE punished after the fact, needing a prosecution; it is defined widely, reaching crew and stowage. Unsafe is a TRIGGER FOR A POWER - provisional detention before the fact, on an opinion honestly formed - and is defined narrowly by listed causes: defective hull, equipment or machinery, or overloading or improper loading. EVERY UNSAFE SHIP IS UNSEAWORTHY, BUT NOT THE CONVERSE.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the two defences to the offence of sending an unseaworthy ship to sea?
retrieval_cards.answer: That he used ALL REASONABLE MEANS to ensure her being sent to sea in a seaworthy state; or that sending or taking her to sea in that state was, in the circumstances, REASONABLE AND JUSTIFIABLE - with the burden of proof on him. There is also a procedural protection: no prosecution is instituted except by, or with the consent of, the Central Government.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What happens when a ship is detained as unsafe?
retrieval_cards.answer: She is PROVISIONALLY detained for survey, and a written statement of the grounds is served on the master FORTHWITH. A survey follows by a surveyor or competent person appointed for the purpose. On the report she is either released or FINALLY detained until the defects are made good. Where a ship has been detained without sufficient reason, COMPENSATION is payable - the discipline on a power exercisable on opinion rather than proof.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the owner's obligation to the crew with respect to seaworthiness, and say what makes it unusual.
retrieval_cards.answer: To use all reasonable means to ensure the ship's seaworthiness for the voyage at the time when it commences, AND TO KEEP HER IN A SEAWORTHY CONDITION DURING IT. What makes it unusual: it is IMPLIED into every contract of service with the master or a seaman and every contract of apprenticeship; it operates NOTWITHSTANDING ANY AGREEMENT TO THE CONTRARY, so it cannot be signed away by the person it protects; and it binds the owner, the master AND any agent charged with loading, preparing or despatching the ship.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the owner guarantee the ship's seaworthiness?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The statutory standard is ALL REASONABLE MEANS, not a guarantee - the Act does not make the owner an insurer of the ship's condition. It is the same standard as the first defence to the offence, and the two provisions read together. But the duty is CONTINUING: a defect arising at sea and ignored is a breach, which is why the planned maintenance system, the defect list and the reporting of defects to the company are how the duty is actually performed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Merchant Shipping Act governs at a July 2023 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, and there is nothing else in the field. Its replacement did not exist in any form at that date - not as an Act, and not as a Bill before either House. The Bill was introduced only in December 2024, seventeen months later, and the Act that repealed the 1958 Act commenced in March 2026.
